weight_of_future_people.theme: How much moral weight future people should carry in present ethical reasoning, relative to people alive now.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Future people matter morally just as much as present people. Where you sit in time doesn't determine how much your suffering or flourishing counts — that's a basic impartialist commitment that almost everyone accepts when stated abstractly. And once you accept it, the numbers do the work: there could be vastly more people in the future than there are now or have ever been, and giving their welfare its due weight pulls the moral center of gravity decisively toward the long-term. The discomfort with this conclusion comes from how unfamiliar it feels, not from any principled reason to discount future welfare.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists usually grant the principle that future people matter, then resist its implications by appealing to uncertainty or to the special weight of identifiable victims. But that's having it both ways. If you genuinely think future people count, the sheer numbers force the conclusion that they dominate the moral calculus. Resisting that conclusion requires either denying the premise — which neartermists usually don't want to do openly — or smuggling in a temporal discount rate that no one would defend if it applied across human individuals at a single time.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The impartialist commitment that suffering counts equally regardless of who suffers extends naturally to when they suffer; temporal partiality is hard to defend in principle.
Estimates of future population, even very conservative ones, dwarf present population by orders of magnitude, which means even modest weight on the future swamps near-term considerations.
Most of the value in human history, on any reasonable reckoning, lies in the future; treating that as a side issue gets the proportions exactly wrong.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Present and near-future people deserve overwhelming ethical priority over speculative future populations. The abstract impartialist move — counting all possible lives equally — sounds principled but produces conclusions no one actually lives by, and the conclusions it produces are mostly bad ones. Concrete present suffering is real, tractable, and morally urgent. Future welfare matters, but the weight you give it has to be proportional to your ability to actually predict and affect it, which is much smaller than longtermists assume. Anchoring ethics in the present isn't a failure of impartiality; it's a recognition of what we can actually know and do.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists treat 'all possible future lives count equally' as a starting axiom and then claim their conclusions follow inevitably. But the axiom does almost all the work, and it's far from obvious. We don't owe the same things to identifiable present people as to abstract possible future ones, and the philosophical tradition has known this for a long time. When the axiom produces conclusions like 'don't help the present poor because expected value of x-risk work dominates,' the right response is to question the axiom, not to embrace the conclusion.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Concrete present harms are knowable, tractable, and morally urgent in ways that speculative future welfare isn't.
Most ethical traditions across history have recognized special obligations to identifiable people, present community, and immediate consequences — that's not a bias to overcome.
The longtermist conclusion that present poverty matters less than speculative x-risk work is a reductio of the axiom that produces it, not an insight.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: If suffering is bad, it's bad whenever and to whoever it happens. Putting that simple thought together with the basic numerical fact that the future could contain orders of magnitude more people than the present is what generates the longtermist position. There's nothing exotic about either premise: temporal impartiality is something nearly everyone endorses when asked directly, and demographers don't actually disagree that humanity could go on for a very long time. What's striking is how quickly the conclusion follows once you take both premises seriously. Most resistance to longtermism, in my experience, is reluctance to follow through on commitments people already implicitly hold.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The standard neartermist move is to say something like 'I do care about the future, but...' and then list reasons we shouldn't actually act on that care. The reasons usually come down to either uncertainty (which I'll grant exists, but which doesn't drive credences to zero) or special weight for identifiable people (which is a feeling rather than an argument). What's missing is a defense of why temporal distance, specifically, should count as a moral weakener when spatial distance doesn't. Without that defense, the neartermist position is a temporal partiality that hasn't been justified, just inherited.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Almost everyone, asked directly, agrees that a person's location in time doesn't change how much their pain or pleasure morally counts — and that simple agreement is enough to anchor longtermism.
The expected number of future people, even on conservative projections, is enormous compared to the present; modest credence in this number is enough to dominate near-term considerations.
On any honest accounting, most of the moral stakes in human history lie ahead of us, not behind us; ignoring that is parochialism dressed up as practicality.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: What we owe is owed to particular people in particular relations, and those relations exist now, not in projected futures. Trying to extend our moral reach across millennia turns ethics into a kind of accounting exercise where abstract numbers about possible future welfare swamp everything we can actually see and act on. The result isn't more impartial — it's just less in contact with the actual moral world. There's something morally serious about staying close to identifiable suffering, present community, and immediate consequence. That's not provincialism; that's where ethics has always been grounded.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermism dresses up an unusual moral position — that abstract numbers about projected populations should determine present priorities — as the inevitable conclusion of impartialist premises everyone shares. But the premises don't force the conclusion; the conclusion follows only if you also accept that abstract aggregation is what ethics is fundamentally about. That's a contested philosophical position, not a neutral starting point, and the moral traditions skeptical of it have good reasons for that skepticism. Calling those reasons 'temporal partiality' is rhetoric, not refutation.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Ethics has always been about particular relations between particular people; longtermism asks us to replace that with abstract aggregation, which is a much weaker grounding.
Identifiable present suffering generates moral demands that abstract projections can't match in either urgency or knowability.
When the impartialist premises produce conclusions that flatten present injustice next to speculative future welfare, the right move is to revisit the premises, not to accept the conclusions.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The case for taking future people seriously is built from two thoughts almost everyone accepts. First: when someone is harmed or benefited matters less than whether they're harmed or benefited at all — pain is pain, joy is joy, regardless of when it happens. Second: the future could plausibly contain enormous numbers of people, far more than have ever lived. Put those together and you get longtermism, more or less. The conclusion can feel jarring because most ethical reasoning happens at human scales, but the philosophical machinery used to reach it is just impartiality plus arithmetic. Refusing the conclusion means rejecting one of those moves, and the second one is hard to reject without denying basic facts about scale.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Most neartermist arguments turn out to be arguments against impersonal aggregation in general, not against longtermism specifically. If you don't think aggregate welfare matters, you don't think it matters across distance, across populations, or across time. Fine — that's a position. But neartermists usually don't want to go there; they want to keep impersonal aggregation for present-tense applications and disable it specifically for future people. That asymmetry is what needs justifying, and the justifications offered (uncertainty, identifiability) don't track temporal distance specifically — they track other things, and importing them into the temporal case is doing the work the argument was supposed to do on its own.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Temporal impartiality — the idea that when something happens doesn't change how much it morally counts — is a thin and widely-shared commitment, not an exotic philosophical position.
Conservative population projections still produce numbers that dominate the moral calculus when given any reasonable weight; the dominance isn't a quirk of optimistic forecasting.
The conclusion that the long-term future morally outweighs the short term is what you get when you take widely-held principles seriously rather than discounting them when convenient.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Anchoring ethics in present and near-future people isn't a failure of impartialist nerve; it's the recognition that moral knowledge runs out at some horizon. We can know a lot about the suffering of people alive now and the consequences of policies in the next several decades. We can know much less about populations centuries out, and almost nothing about populations millennia hence. Ethics that pretends otherwise — that treats projections of trillions of future lives as comparable in epistemic standing to data about present suffering — is reaching beyond what we can actually know. The right response to this epistemic limit is to keep ethics grounded in the horizons where we can act with knowledge.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist response to the epistemic-limits worry is to invoke expected value: even if we can't know much about the long term, we can multiply small credences by huge populations and get large numbers. But this is exactly where the framework breaks down. Multiplying weakly-grounded probabilities by speculatively-projected populations doesn't produce reliable expected values; it produces numbers that look quantitative while resting on layers of guesswork. The expected-value framing borrows the prestige of decision theory without meeting its conditions, and the conclusion that 'future people dominate' is downstream of that abuse.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Moral knowledge runs out at some horizon; honest ethics is grounded in horizons where we can actually know enough to act, not in projections that exceed that.
Expected-value frameworks need well-characterized probabilities and outcomes to produce reliable answers, and longtermist applications meet neither condition.
The dominance of future-people considerations in longtermist arithmetic is downstream of multiplying weakly-grounded numbers — it's an artifact of the framework, not a discovery.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Most people, asked whether the time at which someone suffers should change how much that suffering matters morally, will say no — and they'll mean it. That's the impartialist commitment, and once it's in place, longtermism follows almost mechanically. Future populations are likely to be very large; even if you assign substantial credence to the possibility that they won't be, the expected number of future people remains enormous. Combine those two observations and the moral weight tilts heavily toward the long term. What feels like a strange conclusion is just the consequence of two ordinary commitments meeting each other.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists push back, the pushback usually targets the practical implications — 'this can't be right, it would mean we should focus on x-risk over poverty' — rather than the underlying principles. But practical implications can't be a refutation of principles unless you have a separate argument for why those implications are wrong. And the separate arguments tend to be about what's tractable, not about what's morally weighty. Tractability is a real consideration, but it cuts in different directions for different interventions; treating it as a blanket reason to ignore long-term considerations confuses 'hard to act on' with 'low priority.'
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The impartialist principle (suffering counts equally regardless of when it happens) is one most people endorse on reflection; longtermism just takes it seriously.
Even substantial uncertainty about future population sizes leaves expected populations large enough to dominate the moral arithmetic with any reasonable weighting.
Neartermist resistance usually targets the conclusions rather than the premises; if the premises are widely shared, that's a sign the neartermist resistance is unprincipled.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The longtermist case treats abstract aggregation as the obvious framework for ethics and treats temporal partiality as the burden of proof on the other side. That gets the philosophical situation backwards. Most ethical traditions have recognized that moral obligations are denser between people in actual relation — closer in space, time, kinship, community — than between strangers separated by all of those. Longtermism wants to treat this entire tradition as a parochial bias to overcome, but it's better understood as a serious moral insight about where ethical obligation gets its grip. Ethics anchored in actual relation isn't a failure to be impartial; it's a recognition of what makes moral demands real.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists frame their position as 'taking impartiality seriously' and the alternative as 'temporal partiality.' But the framing presupposes that impersonal aggregation is the default and special relations are the deviation. Most ethical traditions treat the situation in exactly the opposite way: special relations generate the obligations, and aggregation across strangers is a derivative move with its own conditions. Longtermism inherits a particular metaethical position — strong impersonal consequentialism — and treats that position as a starting point rather than a contested view. Once you recognize the inheritance, the case for following longtermism's conclusions weakens substantially.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: The denseness of obligation between people in actual relation isn't a partiality bias to overcome; it's a recognition of what makes obligations real and demanding.
Most ethical traditions across history treat impersonal aggregation as a derivative move with its own conditions, not as the default framework that longtermism assumes.
Taking longtermism's premises as 'just impartiality' obscures that they include a contested metaethical position about impersonal aggregation.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: I'd put it this way: future people will exist, will be conscious, will suffer and flourish in real ways, and our actions affect them. Once you accept those four claims — and almost everyone does — longtermism is essentially the position that takes them seriously. Numbers matter. The fact that there will probably be many more future people than present ones isn't a speculative claim; it's a baseline expectation given any reasonable trajectory for civilization. Weighing those numbers honestly produces a moral picture in which the long-term future is where most of what matters happens. This is what taking ethics seriously across time looks like.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The neartermist position depends on the move that's hardest to defend openly: that some discount on future welfare is warranted, where the discount isn't grounded in uncertainty or tractability but in the simple fact that those people aren't here yet. Stated baldly, that position is hard to defend — almost no one wants to say in print that future people just count for less because they're future. So neartermists tend to gesture at uncertainty instead, and let the discount sneak in as a side effect of epistemic humility. But uncertainty doesn't translate into a discount; it translates into an expected-value calculation, which usually still favors longtermism.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Future people will be fully conscious, fully real, and fully affected by present actions; their not-yet-existing status doesn't reduce their eventual moral standing.
Numerical projections of future population are expected to be much larger than the present, on essentially any reasonable trajectory.
The neartermist discount on future welfare is hard to state in principled terms; it usually appears as a side effect of other moves rather than as a defended position.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The honest position is that we don't owe the same things to abstract possible future people as we owe to identifiable present people. The relationship is different — different in moral character, not just in epistemic accessibility. Present people stand in actual relations to us, with claims that arise from those relations. Future people, especially those many generations out, are participants in scenarios we project onto an unknown world. Ethics has always recognized that these aren't the same kind of moral situation. Longtermism's impersonal-aggregation move flattens them, but the flattening is a philosophical choice with significant costs, not a correction of an obvious error.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists sometimes respond to the actual/possible distinction by saying it's 'just temporal bias.' But the response misses what the distinction is doing. Actual people have particular needs, particular contexts, particular claims that arise from being in relation. Possible future people have whatever projections we attach to them. Treating both as equivalent abstract welfare-bearers — interchangeable units in a consequentialist calculation — drops out the texture that makes ethical relation morally serious. The flattening is the move, and it's the move that needs defending, not the resistance to it.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Present people stand in actual relations that ground particular claims; possible future people are participants in projected scenarios — these are different moral situations.
The flattening of actual and possible into 'welfare-bearers' is a contested philosophical move, not a default position.
Ethical relation has texture (particular needs, particular contexts) that abstract aggregation can't preserve — and that texture is part of what makes obligations morally real.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Consider what it would mean to deny longtermism in the simplest possible form. You'd have to either deny that future people will be morally real (which seems false), deny that there will likely be lots of them (which seems false), or deny that we should care equally about people regardless of when they live (which is the temporal-partiality move that's hard to defend in print). Each of these denials has a heavy burden. The longtermist conclusion isn't an exotic position; it's the default that emerges once you decline to make any of those denials. The resistance to it usually comes from intuitions about where ethics 'should' be focused, not from arguments against any of these three claims.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: What I find unsatisfying about the neartermist position is that it usually accepts the premises and resists the conclusion, without giving an account of which step in the argument fails. Either future people morally count or they don't. Either there will likely be a lot of them or there won't. Either temporal location matters morally or it doesn't. Neartermists tend to grant the first and second, then resist the third without owning that resistance. If you think temporal location does matter morally — that future suffering counts less just because it's future — then you should defend that view explicitly, because it's the actual disagreement. The hedge-and-resist pattern obscures what's being argued.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The premises of longtermism (future people are morally real, there will likely be many, time of existence shouldn't change moral status) are each individually difficult to deny.
Resistance to longtermism usually accepts the premises but rejects the conclusion, which means the resistance is implicitly committed to denying one of the premises without saying which.
Temporal partiality — the move neartermists usually rely on — is hard to defend explicitly; its appeal is mostly that it's left implicit.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Strong longtermism asks us to reorder our moral priorities so that abstract projections of future welfare dominate concrete present harm. But this isn't actually the position that 'falls out' of impartialist premises — it requires a number of additional commitments that aren't widely shared. It requires accepting impersonal aggregation as the framework for ethics, accepting that low-probability astronomical-stakes claims should drive present action, and accepting that we can meaningfully predict and intervene on long-term outcomes. Each of these is contested, and the longtermist case only works if all three go through. Treating the conclusion as inevitable, given just impartialist premises, papers over how much philosophical work is being done.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist argumentative strategy is to present the conclusion as 'just impartiality plus numbers,' so that resistance has to look like temporal partiality. But the conclusion actually requires a lot more than impartiality and numbers: it requires a particular framework for aggregation, a particular response to deep uncertainty, and a particular view about long-term tractability. Each of these can be reasonably contested without rejecting impartiality at all. Naming the additional commitments dispels the impression that resistance is unprincipled, and shows that the disagreement is over substantive philosophical questions rather than over a basic moral premise.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: The longtermist conclusion requires impersonal aggregation, expected-value reasoning at extreme scales, and confidence in long-term tractability — three contested commitments, not just impartiality.
Reasonable disagreement on any of these three commitments is enough to undercut the longtermist conclusion, without rejecting impartiality.
Treating the longtermist conclusion as 'just impartiality plus numbers' obscures the philosophical work the additional commitments are doing.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: There's an old idea, going back to Sidgwick and developed extensively by Parfit, that morality is fundamentally about reducing suffering and increasing flourishing wherever they occur — across time, space, and species, without favoritism for the close at hand. Longtermism is what this idea looks like when you take seriously how much of the relevant suffering and flourishing is going to happen in the future rather than the present. The numbers genuinely are enormous; even modest credence in long-run civilizational continuation produces moral stakes that swamp present-tense considerations. The conclusion is unfamiliar, but unfamiliarity isn't an argument. The framework is the same impartialist consequentialism that produces uncontroversial conclusions in other contexts.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists sometimes object that longtermism's conclusions are unintuitive — that we shouldn't reorder our priorities so that speculative future welfare dominates present concerns. But this is asking the conclusion to match prior intuitions, which isn't really what good moral philosophy is supposed to do. If the premises are sound and the reasoning is valid, the conclusion is what we should update toward, not what we should test our premises against. The 'this conclusion is too strange' move is a refusal to update, not a refutation. Most major moral progress has involved exactly this kind of update against initial intuition.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Impartialist consequentialism, in the Sidgwick/Parfit tradition, is the framework that produces uncontroversial conclusions in many other moral domains; longtermism is the same framework applied across time.
The premise that suffering counts equally regardless of when it happens is widely accepted; the application to the future just follows from taking the premise seriously.

Major moral progress has historically required updating against initial intuition (universal human rights, animal welfare, etc.); rejecting longtermism on intuition-mismatch grounds is methodologically suspect.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The neartermist position, properly developed, isn't a rejection of impartialism — it's a more careful account of what impartialism actually requires. Real impartiality means weighing all the considerations honestly, including the considerable uncertainty about long-term effects, the limits of our ability to predict what future people will need, and the moral importance of present, knowable suffering. When you do that careful weighing, the case for prioritizing present and near-future people becomes stronger, not weaker. Longtermism's appeal to impartiality is selective: it weights future numbers heavily and discounts uncertainty about those numbers, which is a thumb on the scale, not impartial reasoning.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke Sidgwick or Parfit to justify their position, they tend to elide a distinction these philosophers actually drew. Both recognized that obligations to future people are conditional on those people existing, on our actions reaching them, and on our being able to predict what they need. None of those conditions are clearly satisfied for the long-term-future cases longtermism uses. Reading the tradition as straightforwardly endorsing strong longtermism is a kind of philosophical rebranding — taking the parts that support the conclusion, leaving out the parts that complicate it.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Real impartiality requires weighing uncertainty about long-term effects honestly; longtermism's framework systematically underweights this.
The Sidgwick/Parfit tradition recognized that obligations to future people are conditional on existence, reach, and predictability — conditions longtermism papers over.
Selectively invoking impartialism for future-population-weight while ignoring its conditions is a thumb on the scale, not careful philosophy.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Imagine the future stretches out for millions of years, with civilization continuing in some form, and consider all the moral weight that would be in that future — all the suffering, all the joy, all the lives. Now compare that to the moral weight of the present moment. Even if you discount the future heavily for uncertainty, even if you assume many things go wrong along the way, the future-side of the comparison is still vastly larger than the present side. That comparison is what longtermism is responding to. It's not that the present doesn't matter; it's that when you actually weigh the magnitudes, the long-term future is where most of what matters lives. Refusing to act on that recognition is choosing not to follow through on principles you already hold.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: I think a lot of neartermist resistance is failure of imagination — not in a pejorative sense, just descriptively. We can vividly picture present people; we can't easily picture trillions of future ones. The moral intuitions that come from vivid pictures favor present people because they're the ones we can picture. But moral importance isn't determined by what we can picture. The same logic that says 'people in distant countries matter even though I can't see them' extends naturally to 'people in distant futures matter even though I can't picture them.' Resisting that extension requires explaining why temporal distance is different from spatial distance in a way that justifies discounting, and the explanation never quite materializes.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Honest comparison of future moral weight versus present moral weight, even with heavy discounts for uncertainty, gives the future a much larger share.
Resistance to longtermism often comes from imaginative limits — we can't picture the future as vividly — rather than from principled disagreement.
The logic that extends moral concern across spatial distance applies just as cleanly across temporal distance; resisting the latter requires a separate argument that doesn't materialize.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The longtermist 'imagine the moral weight of the future' move is doing more work than it admits. We're not actually imagining moral weight; we're multiplying conjectured population numbers by conjectured welfare estimates and producing a number that we then compare against present moral weight. The comparison feels intuitive because the number is large, but the largeness is a function of what we put into the projection — population estimates, welfare assumptions, civilizational-continuation probabilities. Each input is shaky; the output inherits the shakiness. Calling this 'comparing moral weight' lends quantitative respectability to what is actually speculation.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists say 'just imagine the moral weight of the future,' they're treating projected populations as if they were already real and weighing them against actual present people. But the imaginative work is doing all the persuasion. If we restrict ourselves to populations we have evidence for — present and near-future — the moral arithmetic looks very different. The longtermist case depends on importing projected populations into the calculation as if they had the same epistemic standing as present ones, and that import isn't licensed by the evidence. The 'imagine the weight of the future' move is rhetorical, not philosophical.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Comparisons of future moral weight to present moral weight depend on speculative inputs (population, welfare, continuation probability) that don't have the epistemic standing presented.
The intuitive force of the 'enormous future' comparison comes from numerical scale, but the numbers are projections, not evidence.
Restricting moral arithmetic to populations we have evidence for changes the conclusion substantially; the longtermist case requires importing speculative populations.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: I keep coming back to the simple version: a person experiencing suffering or flourishing in the year 4000 will be just as conscious, just as present-to-themselves, just as morally real as a person experiencing the same things now. Their being far away from us in time doesn't reduce that. Once you really sit with that thought, the question becomes how much we can affect their welfare with present actions, and how to weigh those effects against effects on present people. Both questions have honest answers that don't drive future-welfare to zero. The longtermist conclusion — that the long-term future deserves serious moral attention, often more than we currently give it — follows from that.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists often take the position that we can't meaningfully affect long-term outcomes, so longtermism is moot. But this is empirically wrong for at least some categories of action: catastrophic risks, foundational technology development, long-lived institutions. We have evidence that present action affects these in long-horizon ways. The 'we can't affect the long term' claim is too strong; what's true is that we can't affect every aspect of the long term. The narrower true claim doesn't support the broad neartermist conclusion. It supports a more careful longtermism that focuses on the categories where present action does have long-horizon leverage.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: A person experiencing suffering or flourishing in the distant future is just as morally real as one experiencing it now; temporal distance doesn't reduce moral status.
Empirically, we can affect long-term outcomes in some categories (catastrophic risks, foundational technologies, institutions) — the 'we can't affect the long term' claim is too strong as stated.
The narrow true claim about long-term unaffectability supports more careful longtermism, not blanket neartermism.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Future people will be morally real if and when they exist, but our access to them is fundamentally different from our access to present people. We don't know what their needs will be, what circumstances they'll face, or what our present actions actually deliver to them through long causal chains. This isn't a quibble about uncertainty; it's a structural feature of the temporal-distance relation. Treating future people as morally equivalent to present people, for purposes of action, requires assuming we have access to them that we don't actually have. Realistic ethics works within the access we have, which means weighting present and near-future people much more heavily.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist response — that we can affect long-term outcomes in some categories — is true but doesn't carry the weight the framework needs. Yes, we can plausibly affect catastrophic-risk probabilities and long-lived institutions. But 'plausibly affect' is a weak relation when the populations affected are speculative and the magnitudes of effect are uncertain. The framework requires not just that we can affect long-term outcomes, but that we can confidently weigh those effects against effects on present people. The latter requires much more than the former, and it's the latter the framework actually needs.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Our access to future people is structurally different from our access to present people; we don't know their needs, circumstances, or what our actions deliver to them.
Realistic ethics works within the access we have; longtermism requires confident comparison across access-asymmetric relations.
Affecting long-term outcomes in some categories is true but doesn't license confident weighting against present-tense effects, which is what the framework actually needs.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The strongest case for longtermism, to my mind, isn't the dramatic 'trillions of future lives' framing. It's more modest: even small probabilities of serious effects on the long-term future matter enough to warrant attention, given how much could be at stake. We don't need confident projections of trillions of flourishing future people. We just need to take seriously that catastrophic outcomes would be very bad, that some present actions affect their probability, and that this combination warrants more attention than near-term-only frameworks give it. The astronomical-numbers version of longtermism is one way to make the case; the modest version makes the case more reliably and is harder to dismiss.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists argue against longtermism, they often argue against the strongest version — the 'trillions of lives' calculation — and treat the conclusion as if rejecting that calculation rejects all longtermism. But there's a more modest case that doesn't depend on confident projections of huge future populations. It just requires taking seriously that the long-term future has moral stakes worth attending to, and that present actions can affect it. This modest case survives most neartermist objections, and it's enough to support the practical conclusions longtermism cares about — investing in catastrophic-risk reduction, taking civilizational stability seriously, doing research on long-horizon ethics. Defeating the strong version doesn't defeat the modest one.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: A modest version of longtermism, requiring only that long-term effects matter at all and that present actions can plausibly affect them, supports most of the framework's practical conclusions.
The astronomical-numbers version is rhetorically powerful but philosophically vulnerable; the modest version is more robust to neartermist objections.
Attacks on longtermism that target the strong version don't defeat the modest version; the practical recommendations come through either way.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'modest' version of longtermism is harder to argue against, but that's because it's harder to disagree with — it boils down to 'long-term considerations should matter some.' Almost all neartermists agree with that. The interesting disagreement is over how much, and the modest version doesn't actually answer that question. The strong version of longtermism gives a definite answer (long-term considerations should dominate present ones), and that answer is what neartermism resists. Defending modest longtermism while keeping strong longtermism's policy conclusions is a way of getting the conclusions cheaply, by defending the version that's harder to attack while implementing the version that's harder to defend.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: There's an argumentative pattern in longtermist work where the strong version (trillions of lives, dominate the moral calculus) drives the policy conclusions while the modest version (long-term matters some) does the philosophical defense. The pattern lets longtermists keep all the action-guiding bite of the strong view while only having to defend the much milder modest view. But the policy conclusions don't follow from the modest view — they follow from the strong one. If the strong one is what's actually driving the practical recommendations, then it's the strong one that needs defending, regardless of how the philosophical chapter introduction is written.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: The 'modest' version of longtermism is hard to disagree with but doesn't yield the framework's distinctive policy conclusions.
The strong version yields the policy conclusions but is much harder to defend; longtermism gets argumentative advantage by sliding between the two.
Honest defense of longtermist policy requires defending the strong version that actually drives the conclusions, not the modest version that survives objections.

x_risk_priority.theme: Whether reducing existential risk should be among the highest moral priorities of the present.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Reducing existential risk is among the highest moral priorities the present generation faces. The logic is simple: an existential catastrophe doesn't just kill everyone now — it eliminates the possibility of all future generations, which is where most of the moral value lies. Even small reductions in the probability of such catastrophes have astronomical expected moral value, far exceeding nearly any other intervention. Treating x-risk work as a niche concern, when humanity now has the capacity to end its own future, gets the moral proportions wildly wrong.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists often dismiss x-risk work as speculative, as though we don't know whether nuclear weapons exist or whether engineered pathogens are possible. But the specific risks aren't speculative — they're the well-documented downside of technologies humans have actually built. The 'speculative' label is doing rhetorical work, treating the question of whether to take catastrophic downsides seriously as if it were the same as predicting the far future in detail. It isn't.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The asymmetry of x-risk — recoverable harms vs. unrecoverable extinction — gives prevention astronomical expected value, even at low probabilities.
Specific risks (nuclear, biological, AI) are documented and tractable, not speculative in the way longtermism's critics suggest.
Most of human history's moral value lies in our future; ending it permanently is the worst thing that could happen, by a wide margin.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Existential risk shouldn't dominate present moral priorities. The 'expected value of x-risk work is astronomical' argument depends on probability estimates that no one can actually justify, multiplied by future-population estimates that are essentially made up, discounted by tractability assumptions that are also made up. What you get out is a number that confirms what longtermists already wanted to do. Meanwhile, present harms — global poverty, preventable disease, mental health, ongoing injustice — are real and addressable now. The case for prioritizing the speculative over the actual hasn't been made.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist case for x-risk priority rests on three claims, each of which is shaky: that x-risk probabilities can be meaningfully estimated, that future populations of trillions can be meaningfully predicted, and that present interventions can meaningfully shift the probabilities. Each claim individually deserves skepticism; their conjunction is wildly unsupported. Treating that conjunction as an obvious moral framework rather than a contested philosophical position is the central error of the view.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Probability estimates for civilizational catastrophe, future-population sizes, and intervention tractability are all weakly grounded; multiplying them produces overconfident conclusions.
Present harms are concretely measurable and addressable; reallocating from those to speculative interventions has high opportunity cost.
The 'astronomical expected value' argument was used historically to justify many bad policies; the form of the argument doesn't track actual moral wisdom.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: What makes existential risk different from other catastrophic risks is the asymmetry: a recoverable disaster, however terrible, leaves the future intact, while an unrecoverable one closes it permanently. That asymmetry alone is enough to put x-risk reduction at or near the top of present moral priorities. We don't need exact probability numbers; we just need to take the asymmetry seriously. The work the present generation can do to reduce these risks is uniquely high-leverage in a way that almost no other moral work is, simply because no other present action affects the entire trajectory of what comes next.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists call x-risk work speculative, they often elide the difference between two questions. One is whether the specific technologies that could cause civilizational catastrophe exist — which they manifestly do. The other is whether we can estimate exact catastrophe probabilities — which we can't, but we don't need to. Working to reduce well-understood pathways to civilizational harm doesn't require precise risk estimates; it requires acknowledging that the pathways are real and that the downsides are uniquely bad.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The recoverable-vs-unrecoverable asymmetry alone, without precise probabilities, is enough to put x-risk at the top of present priorities.
Specific civilizational risks (nuclear, biological, AI alignment) trace back to documented technologies and well-understood pathways, not speculation.
Present action has uniquely high leverage on long-term outcomes through x-risk reduction, in a way that few other moral interventions do.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Granting x-risk work the status longtermists want for it requires accepting a chain of weakly-grounded estimates as if they were established science. Each link — probability of catastrophe, sensitivity of probability to present action, magnitude of long-term effect — is uncertain, and the chain inherits the uncertainty multiplicatively. The result is a framework that promises rigor but actually rests on stacked guesswork. Meanwhile, present harms with known causal mechanisms and documented intervention effects have been deprioritized in the name of expected-value reasoning that doesn't actually do what it claims.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The case longtermists make for x-risk priority looks rigorous because it uses the language of expected value and probability calculation. But the inputs to those calculations are guesses, not measurements, and combining several guesses doesn't produce a measurement. What looks like decision-theoretic reasoning is closer to moral arithmetic with arbitrary numbers that produce predetermined conclusions. The framework's appearance of rigor is itself the problem.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Each link in the x-risk-priority chain (probability, sensitivity, magnitude) is independently weakly grounded; combining them compounds rather than reduces uncertainty.
Present harms have known causes and well-documented intervention effects; the case for deprioritizing them in favor of speculative work hasn't been made.
The veneer of decision-theoretic rigor in expected-value calculations obscures that the inputs are largely guesses.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Imagine humanity is wiped out — not in a thousand years, but tomorrow. What's lost? Not just the people alive today, terrible as that would be. Everything that would have come after: every life that would have been lived, every problem that would have been solved, every form of flourishing that would have been achieved. That's the scale of x-risk's downside. Now ask: how much should we be willing to spend, as a present generation, to reduce the probability of that outcome? The honest answer is much more than we currently spend, because the magnitude of what's at stake is vastly larger than anything we typically face in moral decision-making.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who reject x-risk priority usually do so by pointing at uncertainty in the probabilities. But this is exactly backwards as a response to a stake of this size. When the downside is permanent loss of everything that could come after, even modest probabilities warrant substantial action. We don't apply the 'too uncertain to prioritize' standard to other low-probability catastrophic risks — we buy insurance, build redundancy, develop preparedness. Treating x-risk as the exception requires a separate argument for why this particular catastrophic risk is different, and that argument doesn't get made.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: What's lost in extinction isn't just present lives but every future generation that would have come after — a stake whose magnitude warrants major present commitment.
We routinely take low-probability catastrophic risks seriously in other domains (insurance, preparedness, redundancy); applying a different standard to x-risk requires separate justification.
Modest probabilities of permanent loss warrant substantial action when the loss is unbounded — this is standard reasoning, not special pleading.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'imagine humanity wiped out' framing is rhetorically powerful but does the philosophical work without earning it. We're not actually evaluating extinction by comparing it to alternatives; we're imagining a maximally bad outcome and noticing that it's bad. That's true but unhelpful. Real moral comparison requires weighing the probability of various outcomes, the cost of interventions, and the opportunity cost of work not done. When you do this honestly, x-risk work has to compete with present-tense work that has known causal mechanisms and known impact, and the competition doesn't obviously favor x-risk.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists invoke the magnitude of extinction's downside as if magnitude alone settled priority. But priority isn't about magnitude alone; it's about expected value, which combines magnitude with probability and tractability. Each of those is uncertain in the x-risk case. Treating magnitude as if it dominates the calculation by itself — 'extinction is so bad that any nonzero probability matters more than any present harm' — is what people sometimes call Pascalian reasoning, and it has known problems. The longtermist x-risk framing depends on ignoring those problems.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Magnitude of extinction's downside is a feature of the problem, but priority requires combining magnitude with probability and tractability — the longtermist framing emphasizes only the first.
Pascalian reasoning structures (low-probability claims about huge stakes dominating decisions) have known philosophical problems; longtermism inherits them.
Honest comparison requires weighing x-risk work against present-tense work with known mechanisms; the longtermist framing tilts the comparison by emphasizing magnitude alone.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: We're the first generation in history that has actually built tools capable of ending human civilization — and we keep building more. Nuclear weapons, engineered pathogens, increasingly powerful AI systems: these aren't speculative, they exist, and they're concentrated in the hands of small numbers of decision-makers. The moral weight of being the generation that built these capabilities, and now has to handle them, is enormous. Treating x-risk reduction as a niche cause when our generation specifically faces these challenges gets the situation exactly wrong. This is what generational moral responsibility looks like in our context.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists frame x-risk as 'speculative,' they're treating well-documented technological capabilities as if they were science fiction. But the relevant pathways aren't speculative — they trace through real laboratories, real weapons stockpiles, real research programs. The speculative-vs-concrete framing collapses when you look at what specifically is being claimed. The risks are real because the technologies are real, and the technologies are real because we built them. Calling careful attention to what we've built 'speculative' is rhetorical.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The relevant x-risk technologies (nuclear, biological, AI) actually exist; the pathways to civilizational catastrophe trace through real capabilities, not speculation.
Our generation specifically faces challenges no previous generation faced — building and managing world-ending technologies — and that creates a distinctive moral responsibility.
The 'speculative' framing depends on conflating technological reality with prediction-of-specific-outcomes; the technologies are documented even if specific scenarios aren't.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The fact that x-risk technologies exist doesn't settle whether x-risk work should be the highest moral priority. We've had nuclear weapons for eighty years without a civilizational catastrophe. The base rates for actual realization of these technological risks, over reasonable time horizons, aren't well-known and aren't necessarily as high as longtermist priority-setting requires. Being the generation with these capabilities does matter, but it doesn't translate cleanly into 'x-risk work dominates other moral priorities.' That translation requires further claims about probabilities and tractabilities that aren't independently supported.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Pointing at the existence of dangerous technologies isn't an argument for x-risk priority; it's an observation about the moral landscape that everyone shares. The actual question is how much present resource should flow toward reducing x-risk specifically, versus other priorities. The longtermist answer depends on probability estimates, sensitivity analyses, and counterfactual claims that go well beyond 'these technologies exist.' Conflating the technology-existence claim with the resource-allocation claim is part of how the framework smuggles in its conclusions.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: The existence of dangerous technologies is widely acknowledged; the disagreement is over priority allocation, which depends on contested further claims.

Base rates for realization of x-risk technologies over reasonable time horizons aren't well-established; eighty years of nuclear weapons without catastrophe is data the framework doesn't fully reckon with.
Conflating 'these technologies exist' with 'x-risk work should dominate priorities' is how longtermism smuggles in its conclusions.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Civilization is fragile in ways that aren't intuitive until you look closely. The combinations of factors that produced advanced human society — relative climate stability, energy availability, institutional capacity, the absence of catastrophic conflict — could break down in ways that take centuries to recover from, if recovery is possible at all. Reducing the probability of such breakdowns is among the most important things present action can do, because the alternative isn't 'civilization continues but worse.' It's a much darker outcome that forecloses futures we can barely imagine. Taking x-risk seriously is taking civilizational fragility seriously.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The neartermist response 'we've survived this far, so the risks must be lower than longtermists claim' is a classic survivorship-bias error. We've survived because, so far, the dice haven't come up the worst way. But we keep rolling them, and the technologies that produce the worst outcomes are accumulating. The argument from past survival doesn't actually update us about future probabilities in the way the response wants — it just shows that we haven't yet experienced the catastrophe whose risk we're worried about.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Civilization depends on combinations of factors (climate, energy, institutions, peace) whose breakdown could be permanent or take centuries to recover from.
Reducing breakdown probability is uniquely high-leverage in moral terms because the alternative isn't 'civilization continues worse' but 'civilization may not continue.'
Past survival is consistent with high underlying probability of future catastrophe; survivorship bias undermines the 'we've made it this far' counter.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Civilization may be fragile in some respects, but the 'one-shot catastrophe' framing oversells the case. Most paths to civilizational collapse are gradual, contested, and admit of intervention along the way. Treating present action as if it has to prevent a single catastrophic event ignores how civilizational outcomes actually unfold. The long-horizon work that genuinely matters — institutional resilience, conflict prevention, infrastructure development — is mostly continuous with neartermist priorities, not opposed to them. Framing it as opposed to present harm reduction is a longtermist polemical move, not an accurate description of the actual work.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists claim x-risk reduction is uniquely high-leverage, they tend to imagine a discrete catastrophic event whose probability we can shift through present-day intervention. But civilizational outcomes are more complex than that. Most plausible paths to bad long-term outcomes involve cascading institutional, social, and environmental factors that admit of intervention all along the way. Work on these factors is largely continuous with present-tense work on poverty, governance, public health, and institutional capacity. The longtermist framing of x-risk as a discrete-event problem requiring specialized intervention is much weaker than it appears.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Most paths to bad civilizational outcomes are gradual and admit of intervention along the way; the discrete-catastrophe framing is overdrawn.
Long-horizon work that genuinely matters (institutions, peace, infrastructure) is largely continuous with neartermist priorities, not opposed to them.
Framing x-risk as requiring specialized intervention separate from present harm reduction is polemical, not descriptive.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The counterfactual impact of x-risk work is enormous in a way that few other interventions can match. If you successfully reduce the probability of civilizational catastrophe by even a small amount, the expected number of future people who avoid that catastrophe is huge. Compare this to the counterfactual impact of, say, donating to a well-run global health charity: real and important, but bounded by the number of present people you can help. Most ethical frameworks endorse acting where counterfactual impact is largest, and on that criterion, x-risk work clearly dominates.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists sometimes respond to the counterfactual-impact argument by saying 'but we can verify the impact of bednets, not of x-risk work.' This is true but doesn't establish what they want it to establish. Verifiability is a feature of impact-measurement, not a feature of impact-magnitude. Choosing only verifiable impacts means systematically underweighting the largest possible impacts in favor of smaller measurable ones. That's an epistemic preference, not a moral one, and it should be defended as such — not presented as if it were a moral argument.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Counterfactual impact of x-risk work is large because successful reduction in catastrophe probability affects huge expected populations.
Most moral frameworks endorse acting where counterfactual impact is largest; on that criterion x-risk work dominates other interventions.
Verifiability of impact and magnitude of impact are different things; preferring verifiable impacts is an epistemic preference, not a moral argument.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The counterfactual-impact argument for x-risk work depends on accepting a particular way of estimating counterfactuals that isn't well-grounded. We don't actually know whether a given intervention reduces catastrophe probability; we don't know by how much; we don't know what the counterfactual world looks like. Compare this to global health work, where we know quite a lot about what the counterfactual would look like. The 'huge counterfactual impact' for x-risk is largely an inference from premises we can't check, while the 'modest counterfactual impact' for present-day work is grounded in evidence we can check.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke counterfactual impact, they treat the speculative inputs as if they had the same epistemic standing as the evidence-grounded ones. But the calculation that gives x-risk work astronomical counterfactual impact runs through speculative probability estimates, speculative population projections, and speculative intervention-effect estimates. Each of these is much weaker than the corresponding inputs for present-day work. The counterfactual-impact comparison is rigged by treating well-grounded numbers and weakly-grounded numbers symmetrically.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: The 'huge counterfactual impact' for x-risk depends on speculative estimates that don't have the epistemic standing of present-day intervention evidence.
Counterfactual impact comparisons that weight speculative numbers symmetrically with evidence-grounded numbers tilt the comparison artificially.
Present-day intervention work has counterfactual estimates we can check; x-risk work mostly doesn't, and the framework doesn't reckon with this asymmetry.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The most concrete way to think about x-risk priority is in terms of technology governance. Powerful technologies — AI, biotech, autonomous systems — are being developed faster than our institutions can manage them. The work of building governance frameworks, alignment research, biosecurity protocols, and similar interventions has long-term leverage that compounds: a slightly better-governed transition through dangerous technological capability has effects that propagate forward indefinitely. This isn't speculation about distant futures; it's recognition that present technology-governance work is among the highest-leverage moral interventions available, because the technologies it governs have such large potential effects.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The neartermist position tends to treat technology-governance work as if it were optional or specialized — something for technical experts, not a serious moral priority. But the technologies in question affect everyone, and the quality of present governance work shapes how societies handle them. Calling this 'speculative' because the long-term effects are uncertain misses that the long-term effects are uncertain because the governance is uncertain — which is exactly why governance work matters. The recursive nature of the situation is why it warrants priority, not why it deserves dismissal.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Powerful technologies are outpacing institutional capacity to manage them; governance work on this gap is among the highest-leverage present interventions.
Technology-governance work isn't speculative — it's concrete present action whose effects propagate forward through institutional design, alignment research, and biosecurity.
The long-term uncertainty of technological outcomes is itself a function of present governance choices; the recursive structure is why governance priority is warranted.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Technology-governance work is important — but framing it as 'x-risk priority' overclaims. Most of the actual gains from technology governance come from improving present-tense outcomes: less harmful AI deployment, better biosecurity for known risks, improved cybersecurity. These are valuable for present and near-term reasons, not because of speculative astronomical-stakes claims about long-term futures. The longtermist framing of governance work as primarily about civilizational catastrophe diverts attention from the tractable near-term wins to speculative long-term ones, which aren't actually what most governance work delivers.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists conflate two different cases for technology governance. Case one: governance is good because it improves present-tense and near-term outcomes (less harm, better function, more equity). Case two: governance is good because it reduces civilizational-catastrophe probability. Both cases have merit, but the first is well-supported and the second is speculative. Longtermists tend to invoke case one for credibility while drawing on case two for priority allocation, and the slippage between the two is part of how the framework justifies preferences that case one alone wouldn't support.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Technology-governance work mostly delivers present-tense and near-term improvements; the longtermist framing of it as primarily about civilizational catastrophe overclaims.

Conflating 'governance reduces near-term harm' (well-supported) with 'governance reduces civilizational-catastrophe probability' (speculative) is part of how the longtermist framework justifies its preferences.
The strongest case for governance work doesn't require longtermist commitments; using longtermism to motivate governance overpromises and underdelivers.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Parfit and Bostrom both, in different ways, argued that the moral significance of human extinction goes beyond the lives lost in the catastrophe itself. Parfit emphasized that extinction precludes everything that could come after — every future of human flourishing or struggle, every consciousness that would have existed. Bostrom developed the 'astronomical stakes' framework that makes this rigorous: the magnitude of what's at stake in x-risk reduction, even on conservative estimates, dwarfs almost any other moral consideration. These aren't fringe philosophers making exotic claims; they're working out the implications of widely-shared premises about the moral weight of future people.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists object to longtermism's x-risk priority, they often argue against the implementation rather than the philosophy. They'll grant that, in principle, extinction is much worse than civilizational decline; they'll grant that future people morally matter; they'll grant that there could be many of them. Then they'll argue that, in practice, present-day x-risk work isn't tractable enough to warrant priority. But this is a specific empirical disagreement, not a philosophical one — and on the empirical question, the case for tractability is at least as strong as the case against.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Parfit and Bostrom developed the philosophical framework for treating extinction as a distinctive moral catastrophe that goes beyond the loss of present lives.
The astronomical-stakes framework makes the priority case rigorous on widely-shared premises about future-people's moral weight.
Neartermist objections often target tractability rather than philosophy; on the empirical tractability question, the case for x-risk work is at least as strong as the case against.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The Parfit-Bostrom framework, however philosophically careful, depends on premises that are far from settled. The 'astronomical stakes' calculation requires assuming that future populations of vast scale are reasonably probable, that their welfare would be substantial, that present action affects their probability or welfare in measurable ways. Each of these is contested. Treating the framework as a rigorous derivation from widely-shared premises overstates the case. The premises are widely shared in some abstract form, but the specific implementations needed for the framework to work require much stronger commitments than 'future people morally matter.'
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Invoking Parfit and Bostrom doesn't settle the philosophical question; it just names the philosophers who developed the strongest version of longtermism. The relevant question is whether the framework they developed is sound, and the answer depends on whether you accept the specific implementation choices: total-welfare maximization, expected-value reasoning at extreme scales, particular projections of future populations. These are contested philosophical commitments, not neutral implementations of widely-shared premises. Citing the tradition doesn't substitute for defending these commitments.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: The Parfit-Bostrom framework depends on contested implementation choices (total-welfare maximization, EV at extreme scales, specific population projections), not just widely-shared premises.
Citing the philosophical tradition doesn't substitute for defending these specific commitments; the tradition doesn't uniquely determine the longtermist conclusions.
The astronomical-stakes calculation overstates how much rigor follows from impartialist premises alone; substantial additional commitments are required.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Think about the opportunity cost of not doing x-risk work. Every year that passes without serious investment in alignment research, biosecurity, nuclear de-escalation, or pandemic preparedness is a year where the underlying capabilities continue to develop without commensurate safety work. The downside of this drift is huge — not just immediate harms but the foreclosure of better long-term trajectories. Present-tense moral work, however valuable, doesn't have this property: not doing it is bad, but the badness is bounded by present-tense effects. X-risk work has unbounded opportunity cost in a way that justifies priority allocation, even when the direct effects are harder to point at.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The neartermist response that 'we should do present harm reduction because the impact is more verifiable' has a hidden assumption: that opportunity costs are zero or near-zero. But opportunity costs are real. Every dollar spent on a present-tense intervention is a dollar not spent on x-risk work, and that opportunity cost has its own moral weight. When the opportunity is something with potentially astronomical expected value, the cost of forgoing it is correspondingly large. Neartermism systematically underweights this opportunity cost by treating present-tense work as if it had no alternative comparison.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Each year without serious x-risk investment is a year where capabilities outpace safety work; the cumulative downside is huge.
Opportunity cost of not doing x-risk work is potentially astronomical; this matters for resource allocation regardless of how verifiable the work's impact is.
Neartermist comparisons systematically ignore opportunity cost, treating present-tense work as if it had no high-stakes alternative.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The opportunity-cost argument cuts both ways and longtermists rarely acknowledge this. Yes, dollars spent on present-tense work could go to x-risk work — but dollars spent on speculative x-risk work could go to evidence-based present-tense work. The framework that treats x-risk work as having astronomical opportunity cost has to also acknowledge that, conditional on x-risk work being mostly ineffective (which is plausible given how speculative it is), the opportunity cost runs the other way. The argument depends on assuming x-risk work is high-impact, which is the conclusion not the premise.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists invoke opportunity cost selectively. They emphasize that not doing x-risk work has unbounded downside, while ignoring that doing speculative work that doesn't actually reduce risk has its own opportunity cost — every present harm not addressed because resources flowed to ineffective long-term speculation. The asymmetric application of opportunity cost is part of how the framework predetermines its conclusions. Honest opportunity-cost reasoning is symmetric: the cost runs in whichever direction the work is actually less effective.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Opportunity cost runs both ways: speculative x-risk work has its own opportunity cost in present harms not addressed.
Longtermist invocations of opportunity cost are selective — emphasizing the cost of not doing x-risk work while ignoring the cost of doing speculative work.
Honest opportunity-cost reasoning depends on knowing which work is actually effective; longtermism assumes its conclusion in the way it deploys the argument.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: When you compare x-risk work to other things people consider serious moral priorities — global health, climate change, animal welfare — the comparison should make x-risk priority obvious. Climate change is bad partly because of its potential to destabilize civilization; x-risk work directly addresses civilizational stability. Global health saves and improves lives now; x-risk work prevents the catastrophic foreclosure of all future lives. Animal welfare extends moral concern beyond the human species; x-risk work extends it across time. None of this is to say the other priorities don't matter, but in scope and stakes, x-risk work is the framework that naturally encompasses and exceeds them.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who reject x-risk priority while embracing climate priority face a tension. Climate change is treated as deserving present resource allocation precisely because of its long-term effects on civilizational stability and welfare. The same reasoning that justifies climate priority — present action affects long-term outcomes, the long-term outcomes are bad enough to warrant action despite uncertainty — applies more strongly to x-risk. Selectively endorsing one and rejecting the other requires a principled distinction that doesn't actually exist.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: X-risk work naturally encompasses what other moral priorities address — civilizational stability (climate), present welfare extended (global health), moral scope expansion (animal welfare).
Neartermists who endorse climate priority face a tension: the same long-term reasoning that justifies climate priority applies more strongly to x-risk.
On scope and stakes, x-risk work exceeds other recognized moral priorities; the priority ordering follows from honest comparison.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Comparing x-risk work favorably to climate change, global health, and animal welfare requires accepting that x-risk work delivers the kind of impact those others deliver. But this is exactly what's contested. Climate change has well-documented physical mechanisms, measurable outcomes, and a track record of intervention effectiveness. Global health and animal welfare have similar evidentiary grounding. X-risk work mostly doesn't. Putting it in the same comparison category as these well-grounded priorities, and then claiming it dominates them, treats it as if it had the same epistemic standing — which it doesn't.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists rank x-risk above climate, global health, and animal welfare, they're not making an apples-to-apples comparison. Climate, health, and welfare work have evidentiary grounding that x-risk work largely lacks. The proper comparison treats epistemic standing as a feature of the comparison, not a separable consideration. When you do that — when you weight not just the magnitude of stakes but the reliability of the case — x-risk work doesn't dominate; it has to compete on different terms, and the terms don't favor it as straightforwardly as longtermists suggest.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Climate, global health, and animal welfare have evidentiary grounding that x-risk work mostly lacks.
Comparing x-risk work to better-grounded priorities treats them as epistemically equivalent when they aren't.
Honest comparison weights both magnitude and reliability; on the second dimension, x-risk work fares much worse than its competitors.

future_generations_concrete.theme: Whether possible future people are morally equivalent to actual present people, or whether actuality matters morally.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Future people will be just as real, just as conscious, and just as affected by our choices as present people are. The intuition that they 'don't really exist yet' and so matter less is a confused intuition: at the time they exist, they will exist fully, with full moral weight. The fact that we're standing at the wrong temporal point to see them now doesn't reduce their moral status. It would be like saying that people on the other side of the world matter less because we can't see them — a position that looks principled but rests on a parochial moral framework.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists sometimes lean on 'actuality' as the morally relevant feature — only people who currently exist count fully — but this commits them to uncomfortable conclusions. It means that policy decisions affecting people not yet conceived have no moral weight at all from a perspective that prioritizes actuality. Almost no one accepts this; everyone agrees that we shouldn't, for example, dump radioactive waste in a way that poisons the next generation. Once you grant that future people matter at all, the argument that they matter less depends on a temporal partiality that no one would defend at length.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: From their own temporal perspective, future people will be present-tense actual; that's the relevant fact about their moral status.
Almost everyone accepts some obligations to future generations (environmental, financial, political); longtermism just takes the principle seriously.
Discounting moral weight by temporal distance is structurally similar to discounting by spatial distance, and we reject the spatial version.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: There's a morally important difference between actual present people and merely possible future people. Actual people have particular needs, particular relationships, and particular claims on us; merely possible people are abstractions, defined entirely by what we project onto them. Treating these categories as morally equivalent — as longtermism does — flattens out a distinction that serious ethics has always recognized. We're related to actual people in a way that grounds moral obligation; the relation we bear to merely possible people is much thinner, and the obligations are correspondingly thinner.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist move is to flatten the actual/possible distinction — to treat future people as 'just as real' as present people — and then to invoke their numbers. But the move depends on the flattening. Once you accept that actual identifiable people have moral standing in a different way than abstract possible populations do, the longtermist arithmetic stops working. The numbers matter only under the assumption they're commensurable with actual people, and that assumption is the thing in question.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Actual people have particular identities, relationships, and claims; merely possible people are abstractions defined by our projections.
Most moral traditions recognize a difference between obligations to identifiable individuals and obligations to faceless aggregates; longtermism erases it.
The flattening of actual/possible is doing real work in the longtermist argument; it's not a neutral starting point.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: When a person exists in the year 3000, they will exist completely, with the same kind of presence and moral standing that present people have now. The fact that we're alive in 2025 and they aren't yet doesn't change anything about their eventual reality. Treating future people as somehow less morally real because they haven't appeared yet is like treating people we haven't met as less real than people we have — a temporary feature of our perspective taken as a fact about them. The right way to think about this isn't to discount future people but to recognize that they will be just as fully present to themselves, and to others around them, as we are now.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who lean on the actuality distinction often back away from its full implications. They want to say future people matter less because they're not actual yet — but they also don't want to say environmental obligations to future generations are weightless, or that we have no reason to avoid leaving radioactive waste for our descendants. The combination is unstable. Either actuality is doing the moral work, in which case obligations to non-actual people are weak, or it isn't, in which case the longtermist case proceeds.
