The neartermist position usually wants the credibility of the latter while using the rhetoric of the former.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: When future people exist, they will be fully present to themselves and to those around them — their not-yet-existing status now is a feature of our temporal location, not theirs.
Neartermist intuitions about not poisoning future generations show that 'actuality' isn't really doing the moral work people think it is.
Treating temporal absence as moral absence treats our perspective as morally privileged in a way no good argument supports.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Actual present people stand in a different moral relation to us than merely possible future people. The relation isn't just about who we can see — it's about the kind of moral demand a person can make on us, which depends on actually existing in shared moral space. A possible future person isn't in shared moral space; they're a placeholder we project into the future, with whatever properties we've imagined them having. Treating that projection as morally equivalent to a person who is here, now, with their own particular needs and history, drops out the texture that makes moral relation morally serious.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists insist 'future people will be just as real,' they're trading on an ambiguity. Yes, when they exist, they'll exist. But what's at stake in moral reasoning now is what relation we bear to them now, and that relation is fundamentally different from the relation we bear to actually existing people. The 'they'll be just as real' move treats existence-at-time-T as if it determined moral standing-from-our-perspective, which it doesn't. The relation matters as much as the existence does, and the relation is the thing that's different.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Moral relation depends on shared moral space, which possible future people don't actually inhabit from our present perspective.
The 'they'll be just as real when they exist' move trades on an ambiguity between existence-at-future-time and moral-standing-from-our-perspective.
Texture of moral relation — particular needs, history, situation — is what makes obligations real; possible future people are defined entirely by projection.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The argument from spatial impartiality applies straightforwardly to time. We don't think people on the other side of the world matter less because we can't see them; we accept that their moral standing is independent of our location. The same reasoning extends to people in distant futures. Their location in time isn't relevantly different from a person's location in space. The intuitions that pull against this extension are the same intuitions that used to pull against extending moral concern to strangers, foreigners, future generations of our own line — intuitions that careful ethical thought has consistently overruled. Longtermism is the next step in the same movement.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who maintain the actuality distinction tend to invoke a sort of moral relativity that doesn't have a principled basis. They say future people are 'less morally real' from our perspective because they're not yet here. But moral status doesn't work that way; it's not perspective-dependent. A person isn't more or less morally real depending on who's evaluating them. The relativity move is a way of getting near-term-favoring conclusions out of impartialist premises, and the relativity itself is what's smuggled in.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Spatial impartiality is uncontroversial; the argument extends straightforwardly to temporal impartiality.
Past extensions of moral concern (to strangers, foreigners, future generations) have followed exactly this pattern; longtermism continues it.
Moral status isn't perspective-dependent in the way the actuality distinction would require; the appeal to 'less real from our perspective' is unprincipled.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The spatial-temporal analogy that longtermists rely on doesn't actually hold. People on the other side of the world are actual; we just can't easily reach them. People in the distant future aren't actual yet, in any sense — they're entirely speculative entities defined by our projections. The right comparison isn't 'spatially distant people' but 'hypothetical people who might exist in some scenarios.' Once you get the comparison right, the analogy stops doing the work longtermists want it to do, and the differential treatment of actual and possible people stops looking like temporal partiality and starts looking like a sound philosophical distinction.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The strongest move in longtermism's playbook is the spatial-temporal analogy: 'we don't discount by space, why discount by time?' But the analogy fails on examination. Spatially distant people exist; we can know facts about them, communicate with them in principle, and verify their welfare. Temporally distant people are projections — defined by our scenarios rather than independently real. The analogy pretends these are the same kind of thing, but they aren't. Recognizing the disanalogy doesn't require defending temporal partiality; it requires only defending the distinction between actual and possible.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Spatially distant people are actual; temporally distant people are projections — the analogy breaks at the most important point.
Spatial impartiality is about people whose existence we know; temporal impartiality is about populations we project onto unknown futures.
Recognizing the disanalogy doesn't require defending temporal partiality; the actual/possible distinction does the work without it.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Consider the case of policy decisions affecting populations not yet born. Almost everyone accepts that we have some obligations here — not to leave nuclear waste that will poison the next century, not to lock in climate trajectories that will harm our descendants, not to design institutions that will cause systematic suffering downstream. These obligations exist because we recognize that future people, when they come to exist, will be morally real in just the way present people are. Longtermism takes this widely-accepted recognition and follows it through to its implications, instead of stopping at conveniently short time-horizons. The structure of the obligation is the same; it's just the scope that's contested.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists try to limit moral concern to actual present people, they have to either accept that we have no obligation to future generations at all (which almost no one wants to say) or carve out exceptions that have to be defended on case-by-case grounds. The exceptions tend to be unprincipled — 'we have obligations to people in 50 years but not 500 years' — without a clear basis for the cutoff. Longtermism is what you get when you decline to make these arbitrary cutoffs and follow the logic of obligation-to-future-generations through to its endpoint.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Almost everyone accepts some obligations to future generations (environmental, institutional, financial); the structure of these obligations extends naturally to longer horizons.
Neartermist exceptions to the actuality principle (we do have obligations to near-term future generations) are unprincipled without a clear basis for the cutoff.
Longtermism is the consistent application of intuitions about future-generation obligations that almost everyone already holds in some form.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Yes, we have some obligations to future generations — but these are different in kind, and weaker in degree, than obligations to present people. Most reasonable people recognize that we shouldn't poison the next generation while also recognizing that we don't owe distant future people the same things we owe our contemporaries. This isn't an arbitrary cutoff; it tracks something real about how moral obligation works. The strength of the obligation depends on the closeness of the relation, the predictability of the impact, and the specificity of the people we're talking about. Longtermism wants to extend obligations to populations that are abstract, distant, and projected — and the extension isn't licensed by the obligations we accept for closer cases.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists treat the existence of any obligations to future generations as a wedge for unbounded extension. 'You agree we shouldn't poison the next generation; therefore you agree future people matter; therefore the longtermist position follows.' But the inferential chain doesn't actually work. Obligations to nearby future generations can be much stronger than obligations to distant ones, for principled reasons (predictability, specificity, relation). Recognizing some obligation to the next generation doesn't commit you to equal obligation to the people of 4000 CE.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Obligations to future generations are stronger for nearby generations and weaker for distant ones, for principled reasons (predictability, specificity, relation).
Recognizing some obligation to the next generation doesn't commit one to equal obligation across all future time — the wedge doesn't work.
Longtermism's inferential extension from 'we owe something to the next generation' to 'we owe equal weight to all future generations' isn't licensed.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: I think the cleanest way to see this is to consider what would happen if we knew, for certain, that humanity would continue for a million years and contain trillions of people. Would those people matter morally? Of course they would. They'd suffer, flourish, love, struggle — everything that makes present people morally real. Now reduce the certainty: even if we're not sure humanity will continue that long, the expected number of future people remains very large. The expected moral weight follows from the expected population. The actual/possible distinction tries to drive this weight to zero based on metaphysical anxiety about non-actual people, but the anxiety isn't warranted — these are projected entities whose moral standing, when they come to exist, will be unaffected by our present uncertainty about them.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who lean on 'these people don't actually exist yet' are usually conflating two different worries. One is metaphysical: there's something philosophically peculiar about possible future people. The other is epistemic: we can't be certain they'll exist. The metaphysical worry doesn't actually undercut moral concern — possible people will be real when they exist, regardless of how we feel about possibility now. The epistemic worry is real but doesn't drive concern to zero; it just translates into expected-value reasoning. Conflating the two lets neartermists get strong conclusions out of weak premises, but the conflation is the move that's actually doing the work.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Future people, when they exist, will be morally real in exactly the way present people are; metaphysical anxiety about possibility doesn't change this.
The 'these people don't exist yet' worry conflates metaphysics (possibility) with epistemics (uncertainty); separating them deflates the actuality argument.
Expected moral weight tracks expected population; uncertainty translates into expected-value reasoning, not zero weight.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The argument 'just consider how many future people there might be' presents the question as if it were settled by counting projections. But projections aren't people. The trillions of future lives that figure in longtermist arithmetic are scenario-dependent populations defined entirely by what we assume will happen. Real people — actual people we have reasons to care about — have texture, particularity, relation. The projected trillions don't. Treating them as equivalent to the second category is flattening that hides what's distinctive about actual moral standing.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists treat future people as if their non-actuality were merely a temporary feature that doesn't matter for moral reasoning now. But the non-actuality matters precisely because all we have to go on are scenarios and projections. The 'they'll be just as real when they exist' framing is true but irrelevant: the question isn't what they'll be when they exist, but what relation we bear to them now, given that they don't exist and may never exist. The relation we bear to projected people is fundamentally different from the relation we bear to actual people, and treating them as equivalent flattens out the distinction.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Projected populations aren't people; the longtermist argument flattens this distinction by treating projections as equivalent to actual people.
The 'they'll be real when they exist' framing answers the wrong question; the right question is about our relation to them now, not their eventual reality.
Texture and particularity of moral standing don't transfer to projections; they're features of actual people, not features all hypothetical entities share.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Take the strong intuition almost everyone shares: we shouldn't take actions that benefit us at the cost of producing suffering for our great-great-grandchildren. Why does this intuition exist? Because we recognize that those people, when they come to exist, will suffer in just the way we'd suffer from analogous actions. Their welfare matters. Now extend the same logic across more generations. The structure of the moral concern is the same — we're recognizing that future suffering or flourishing counts. The fact that we lose track of the people as they get further in time doesn't change what's actually morally at stake. Longtermism is what you get when you don't lose track.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists tend to grant the great-great-grandchildren case, then insist this concern doesn't extend further. But the concern doesn't have a natural cutoff — it's based on the moral reality of future people, which doesn't suddenly diminish past some specific generation. Trying to find a principled reason for stopping the extension typically fails: appeals to predictability work for some long-horizon cases, appeals to relation work for others, but none of them carve out exactly the conclusion 'great-great-grandchildren matter, but not anyone after them.' The neartermist cutoff isn't principled; it's where attention happens to stop.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Intuitions about obligations to nearby future generations (great-great-grandchildren) rest on recognition that future suffering counts; the recognition doesn't have a natural cutoff.
Attempts to ground a cutoff in predictability or relation work for some cases but don't carve out the specific conclusion that obligations stop somewhere.
Where neartermist concern actually stops is more accurately described as where attention stops, not where principled obligation stops.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: There are good reasons to think obligations attenuate with temporal distance even if we don't have a sharp cutoff. Predictability of effects diminishes; specificity of the people involved diminishes; the meaningfulness of the relation diminishes. These attenuations don't require a discrete cutoff to do moral work — they make obligations to nearby future people stronger than obligations to distant future people, in graduated fashion. Longtermism collapses this gradient and treats all future generations as equivalent, but the gradient is real and morally important.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists challenge neartermists to defend a cutoff, they treat the lack of a sharp cutoff as if it implied no gradient. But the gradient doesn't require a sharp cutoff. Obligations to the next generation are stronger than obligations to the generation after; obligations to people in 50 years are stronger than obligations to people in 500. The strength attenuates with temporal distance for principled reasons (predictability, specificity, relation). Longtermism flattens this gradient and then complains that neartermists can't draw a sharp line where the gradient runs out — but the gradient itself, not a cutoff, is what does the moral work.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Obligations attenuate with temporal distance for principled reasons (predictability, specificity, relation), even without a sharp cutoff.
Longtermism's challenge to defend a cutoff misunderstands neartermism's actual structure, which uses a gradient.
The gradient does moral work without a sharp boundary; the demand for a sharp boundary is itself the move that's not licensed.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Here's a thought experiment: if we discovered, today, that an alien civilization existed and would suffer from our actions, we'd recognize obligations to them. We don't share their world; we don't see them; we can't communicate with them. But their existence — their suffering, their welfare — would still ground moral concern. Future people are at least as morally real as such aliens would be. They'll exist; they'll be conscious; they'll be affected by what we do now. The temporal separation isn't doing more moral work than the spatial separation in the alien case. Longtermism asks us to extend to future people the same recognition we'd extend to spatially distant aliens whose existence we acknowledged.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who reject longtermism on actuality grounds usually have to do some careful footwork to avoid implying that morally distant present-day people don't matter either. The structure of their resistance — 'we don't have access, we can't be sure they exist as projected, the relation is too thin' — applies to spatially distant people we've never met as well. If neartermism really did follow consistently from the actuality distinction, it would imply we have no obligations to most of the present-day humans we've never met. Almost no one accepts this, which means the actuality distinction isn't really doing the work.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Hypothetical alien civilizations whose existence we acknowledged would ground moral obligation; future people are at least as real as such aliens.
The relation we have to spatially distant present people we've never met is structurally similar to the relation we have to temporally distant future people.
Neartermist resistance, applied consistently, would deny obligations to most present-day strangers; almost no one accepts this, so the resistance isn't actually principled.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The alien-civilization analogy fails in just the way the spatial-impartiality analogy does. Hypothetical aliens whose existence we discovered would be actual entities — already there, with definite properties and welfare. Future people aren't like that. They're projected entities defined by our scenarios, not independent realities we've discovered. The disanalogy is the same as before: actual entities, however distant, are different from projected ones. Replacing 'spatially distant person' with 'spatially distant alien civilization' doesn't change the relevant disanalogy.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists keep building variants of the spatial-impartiality argument — distant strangers, distant aliens — and the variants all fail at the same point. The cases that work analogically are cases of actual existence at distance. The cases longtermism actually needs are cases of merely possible existence in the future. The analogical move trades on a similarity (distance) while ignoring a difference (actual vs possible). Each variant of the argument has the same structural problem; iterating them doesn't fix it.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Hypothetical aliens we discovered would be actual; the analogy fails because future people are projected, not actual.
Variants of the spatial-impartiality argument (distant strangers, distant aliens) all fail at the same point: actual at distance vs possible.
The longtermist analogical strategy depends on a similarity (distance) that doesn't address the relevant difference (actuality).

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The right way to think about this isn't 'do future people exist now?' (they don't, trivially) but 'will our actions affect them when they do exist?' If yes, then they're in our moral domain. The 'actuality' framing focuses on the wrong temporal relation. We don't generally think moral obligations require our patients to exist at the moment of our deliberation; we think they require our patients to exist at the moment our actions reach them. By that standard, future people are clearly within the scope of moral reasoning, because our present actions reach them. The non-existence-at-deliberation-time is irrelevant.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who emphasize present-tense actuality are usually working with an oddly truncated temporal frame for moral reasoning. We don't think a child not yet conceived has no moral status with respect to actions we take now that will affect them later — that would imply there's no problem with actions whose harm only kicks in after conception. Almost everyone rejects this. The temporal frame for moral concern is 'when our action reaches the patient,' not 'when our deliberation occurs.' Once you adopt the right frame, the actuality argument deflates.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Moral obligation requires patients to exist when our actions reach them, not when we deliberate.
The 'actions whose harm kicks in after conception' case shows the action-time frame is what almost everyone actually uses.
Adopting the right temporal frame for moral concern collapses the distinction between actual-at-deliberation and possible-at-deliberation but actual-at-action-time.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Even granting that the right temporal frame is 'when our actions reach the patient,' there's still a major difference between actions that reach near-term future people (whose existence and welfare we can plausibly anticipate) and actions that reach far-future people (whose existence is conditional on long chains of historical contingency). The frame-shift doesn't deliver the longtermist conclusion; it just relocates the problem. Even within the 'when actions reach patients' frame, far-future people are different from near-future ones because their existence is much more conditional and much less predictable.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists shift the temporal frame from 'when patients exist' to 'when actions reach patients' and treat the shift as if it equalized near and far future. But the shift doesn't equalize; it just moves the problem. Within the action-time frame, near-future patients are still much more knowable, still much more relationally connected to us, still much more particular. The far-future people whose welfare longtermism wants to weight equally remain conditional on long chains of historical contingency. The frame-shift is a clever move but doesn't deliver the equivalence the framework needs.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Even granting the action-time frame, near-future and far-future patients are differently knowable, relational, and conditional.
The temporal-frame argument relocates the actuality problem rather than resolving it.
Far-future people remain conditional on long historical chains in ways near-future people aren't; the action-time frame doesn't erase this.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The argument I find most compelling here isn't metaphysical but practical. We routinely make decisions whose effects extend across generations: constitutional design, infrastructure, environmental policy, technology development. We treat these decisions as morally weighty precisely because they affect people who don't yet exist. Once we've accepted that this weight is real — and we have, in practice — extending it across more generations is just the consistent position. The moral weight is grounded in the future-tense reality of the people affected, not in their present-tense existence. Practice has already moved beyond the actuality distinction; longtermism asks the philosophical position to catch up.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Practitioners of long-horizon work — infrastructure planners, constitutional drafters, environmental scientists — already operate as if future people had moral standing comparable to present people. The neartermist actuality position doesn't match the actual moral practice of these domains. When neartermists insist on the actuality distinction in philosophical contexts while accepting these practices, there's an implicit double standard. Longtermism just asks for consistency: the moral weight that practice already grants future people in long-horizon work, applied across longer horizons.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Long-horizon practice (infrastructure, constitutions, environmental policy) already grants future people moral weight comparable to present people.
The actuality distinction is largely abandoned in practice; longtermism asks philosophy to catch up to the practice.
The double standard between accepted practice and rejected longtermism is itself evidence that the actuality distinction isn't really doing the moral work.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Long-horizon practice grants weight to nearby future generations, not to all future people equally. Constitutional drafters consider the next century, not the next millennium. Infrastructure planners consider the lifetime of the structure, not all subsequent users. Environmental policy considers reasonably foreseeable consequences, not all downstream effects across geological time. The practice isn't 'actuality doesn't matter morally'; it's 'graduated consideration extends to the foreseeable future, attenuated by predictability and specificity.' Longtermism reads this practice as supporting unlimited extension; the practice itself doesn't.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke long-horizon practice, they overinterpret what the practice actually does. Constitutional drafters, infrastructure planners, environmental scientists do extend moral concern across time, but they extend it to foreseeable, specific, relationally-connected futures. They don't extend it to populations of trillions across millennia. Treating the practice as evidence for longtermist universal extension is a category mistake — the practice is graduated, conditional, and bounded in just the ways longtermism wants to abandon.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Long-horizon practice extends moral concern to foreseeable, specific, relationally-connected futures, not to all future people equally.
Constitutional, infrastructural, and environmental practices are graduated and bounded in ways longtermism wants to abandon.
Treating the practice as evidence for unlimited extension misreads what the practice actually does.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: It might help to think about this from the perspective of a future person. Imagine someone a thousand years from now, looking back at our generation. They have their own concerns, their own moral life, their own welfare to protect. They would, presumably, want us to have considered their welfare in our decision-making — not in some abstract sense but in actual, weight-bearing ways. From their perspective, the actuality distinction we're tempted to draw would seem arbitrary and self-serving: they're real to themselves, just as real as we are to ourselves, and the temporal asymmetry between us is just as much our perspective as theirs. The right way to take their interests seriously is to take them seriously now, before they exist.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The future-perspective argument is one neartermists usually have trouble with, because it makes vivid what the actuality distinction actually requires us to say. Telling a future person 'sorry, you weren't actual yet when we made our decisions, so your welfare didn't fully count' isn't a philosophical position most people would willingly defend in propria persona. The neartermist position relies on the abstraction of 'possible future people' to insulate it from this discomfort, but once you imagine the actual future people whose welfare is at stake, the discomfort returns and the position weakens.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: From a future person's perspective, our actuality distinction would look arbitrary and self-serving.
Defending the actuality distinction face-to-face with an actual future person would be uncomfortable for most people; the abstraction of 'possible people' insulates the position from this discomfort.
Taking future people's interests seriously means taking them seriously now, before they exist — there's no other time to do it.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'imagine a future person looking back' move is rhetorically powerful but philosophically slippery. We're not actually consulting a future person; we're imagining what they'd want us to do, projected through our own values. The future people we imagine are versions of us, suitably extended. They would say what we'd want them to say, because they're our projections. Real future people, when they exist, will have their own views, which may or may not match our projections. The 'future-perspective' argument treats imagined preferences as if they were actual ones, which is exactly the move the actuality distinction targets.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists ask us to imagine future people's perspective, they're presenting our own projections as the perspective of independent agents. The future person who 'would want us to consider their welfare' is a version of us, imagined into the future. Treating these projections as if they had independent moral authority is exactly the actuality confusion the neartermist position guards against. Real future people, when they exist, will have views shaped by their own conditions, not by our present-tense imagining of what they'd think. The argument trades on confusing projection with consultation.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Imagined future people are projections of our own values, not independent agents with their own perspectives.
Treating projected preferences as if they had independent moral authority confuses imagination with consultation.
The 'future-perspective' move is rhetorically powerful precisely because it lets us act on our own preferences while attributing them to imagined others.

person_affecting_view.theme: Whether ethics is fundamentally about benefiting and harming particular individuals, or about producing the best aggregate states of affairs.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Ethics is about producing the best states of affairs we can — minimizing suffering, maximizing flourishing — and this commitment, taken seriously, leads to longtermism. The 'person-affecting view' that ethics is fundamentally about benefiting particular individuals creates absurd results: it implies we have no obligation to bring into existence flourishing people, no obligation to prevent extinction (since no one is harmed by not existing), and a host of other counterintuitive implications. The impersonal view — that we should make the world contain more good and less bad — is the framework that actually explains our moral commitments, and it's what supports longtermism.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists often appeal to person-affecting intuitions to resist longtermism: 'no one is harmed if a flourishing future doesn't happen, because no one is there to be harmed.' But this argument proves too much. It implies that creating a miserable population is morally equivalent to not creating a flourishing one, since neither involves harming anyone determinate. Almost no one accepts this. Once you reject the person-affecting view, the door to longtermism opens, and the neartermist resistance runs out of ground to stand on.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The person-affecting view implies that creating happy people has no value, which clashes with most considered moral judgments.
Impersonal aggregation is the framework most consistent with our actual moral commitments about populations, history, and futures.
Once you accept that bringing flourishing people into existence is good, the longtermist conclusion follows quickly.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Ethics is fundamentally about benefiting and harming particular people, not about producing the best aggregate states of affairs. This is what's right about the person-affecting view: morality is grounded in actual relations between actual people, not in some impersonal calculation of total welfare. When longtermism asks us to count merely possible people in the moral arithmetic — to treat their non-existence as a harm to be prevented — it abandons the person-affecting grounding that makes ethics intelligible. What's left is a kind of moral abstraction that nobody actually lives by.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist case for impersonal aggregation depends on counterintuitive cases (the 'making happy people is good' move) and on dismissing the strong intuition that morality is between particular people. But intuitions about particular cases pull strongly the other way: most people don't think we have an obligation to bring as many flourishing people into existence as possible, and don't think non-existence is a harm. Person-affecting views capture these widely-shared moral judgments; the impersonal framework requires us to override them.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Most considered moral judgments are about particular relations between particular people, not impersonal aggregation.
The intuition that we don't owe potential people existence is widely shared and supports the person-affecting framework.
Impersonal aggregation, taken seriously, leads to repugnant conclusions; the person-affecting view avoids them by grounding ethics in actual relations.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Take the person-affecting view seriously and you end up committed to claims most people reject. You'd have to accept that creating a population of happy beings has no positive value at all, since none of them is benefited by being created. You'd have to accept that human extinction isn't intrinsically bad — only the deaths involved are bad, and the absence of subsequent generations is morally neutral. Almost no one really thinks this. The reason is that we're not actually committed to the person-affecting view; we're committed to something more like 'the world is better when it contains more flourishing and less suffering,' and that impersonal commitment is what longtermism builds on.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who lean on person-affecting reasoning try to use it as a tool against longtermism without confronting its other implications. But the view is a package: if you adopt it to block longtermism, you also adopt the conclusion that creating happy beings has no positive value, that ending humanity isn't bad-for-anyone, that asymmetries between creating happy people and creating miserable ones become hard to defend. These implications are widely rejected, which means person-affecting reasoning, used selectively, isn't really the philosophical anchor neartermists want it to be.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Person-affecting reasoning, taken consistently, implies creating happy beings has no positive value — a conclusion almost no one accepts.
The same view implies extinction isn't intrinsically bad, only the deaths involved — also widely rejected.
Selective use of person-affecting reasoning to block longtermism, without accepting its broader implications, is unprincipled.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: What's right about the person-affecting view is that ethics has grip on us through particular relations to particular beings. The reason cruelty is bad isn't that it lowers some abstract welfare-aggregate; it's that it harms a particular sufferer. The reason kindness is good isn't that it raises an aggregate; it's that it benefits a particular person. Ethics is between people, in this sense, not over them. The impersonal framework that longtermism requires treats moral relation as if it were welfare-bookkeeping, which loses the moral substance that makes ethics demanding in the first place.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists treat 'between particular people' and 'over impersonal aggregates' as if they were two equivalent ways of describing the same moral fact. They aren't. The first picks out the actual moral relation that grounds obligation; the second is an abstraction that floats free of the relation. Most ethical traditions throughout history have recognized this and grounded morality in particular relation. Longtermism's impersonal framework abandons that grounding for an aggregation framework, and the abandonment is a real philosophical loss, not a clarifying simplification.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Cruelty and kindness get their moral force from particular relation to particular sufferers and beneficiaries, not from impersonal welfare-bookkeeping.
Most ethical traditions across history ground morality in relation rather than aggregation; longtermism abandons this grounding.
The 'particular vs aggregate' distinction isn't two equivalent framings; one picks out moral relation, the other an abstraction.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Consider the case of preventing a population of flourishing future people from existing — say, by some present action that forecloses the conditions for their creation. The person-affecting view has to say this isn't a harm to anyone, since no one is there to be harmed. But that's an obviously bad answer to give. Of course preventing flourishing populations from existing is morally bad; it's bad because the world would have contained more flourishing if those populations had existed. That moral judgment requires impersonal reasoning — caring about world-states, not just relations between determinate persons. Longtermism is what this impersonal reasoning looks like applied at scale.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who insist on person-affecting reasoning have to bite an uncomfortable bullet: foreclosing flourishing futures is morally neutral on their view, because no determinate person is harmed. They tend to wriggle out of this by saying 'well, present people care about future flourishing' — which is true but doesn't ground the moral fact, just our reaction to it. The clearest sign that we're committed to impersonal reasoning is that foreclosing flourishing futures strikes almost everyone as wrong, and the wrongness is about the foreclosure, not about anyone's reaction to it.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Foreclosing flourishing future populations is widely judged wrong, but the wrongness can't be cashed out in person-affecting terms — it requires impersonal reasoning about world-states.
Person-affecting attempts to ground this judgment in present-people's-preferences shift the locus of wrongness in implausible ways.
The widespread judgment that foreclosing flourishing is wrong shows we're already committed to impersonal reasoning; longtermism makes this commitment explicit.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'foreclosing flourishing futures' case looks like it requires impersonal reasoning, but a careful person-affecting view handles it. What's wrong with foreclosing flourishing futures isn't that some impersonal aggregate is reduced; it's that the actions involved harm or risk harming people who do or will exist along the way. The damage is to actual future people, including ones whose existence depends on the trajectory, not to a non-existent aggregate. Person-affecting reasoning, properly developed, captures the wrongness without invoking impersonal welfare-comparison.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists treat the person-affecting view as if it were obviously committed to denying that foreclosing flourishing is bad. But this overstates what the view actually says. Person-affecting views can recognize that foreclosing futures harms real people whose existence depends on those futures' continuation, even without committing to impersonal welfare-comparisons. The longtermist argument that 'person-affecting reasoning has to deny that foreclosing flourishing is bad' targets a strawman version of the view, not the careful versions actually defended in the literature.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Careful person-affecting views can recognize the wrongness of foreclosing flourishing without committing to impersonal aggregation.
The wrongness of foreclosing futures can be cashed out in terms of harm to people whose existence depends on the trajectory.
Longtermist arguments against person-affecting reasoning often target strawman versions, not the careful versions in the literature.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: If you really thought ethics was only about particular relations between determinate people, you'd have to accept some strange consequences. You'd have to say a world with ten happy people is no better than a world with no people. You'd have to say it's morally permissible to bring miserable beings into existence as long as no determinate present person is harmed by their creation. You'd have to say preventing the existence of a possible flourishing person carries no moral weight at all. These conclusions are hard to defend; almost everyone, on reflection, rejects them. The impersonal framework that does the explanatory work everywhere else — caring about world-states, not just determinate relations — is what supports longtermism.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The neartermist relies on intuitions about particular determinate cases, but person-affecting reasoning produces wildly counterintuitive results in just-as-determinate cases. We can imagine specific scenarios — a flourishing person who never gets born because of a present choice — and the person-affecting view has to say nothing morally significant happened. But this is contrary to almost everyone's considered judgment. The neartermist position isn't really tracking robust moral intuitions; it's tracking some intuitions while running into fierce contradiction with others, and the contradiction is unresolved.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Strict person-affecting reasoning implies a world with ten happy people is no better than an empty world — a conclusion almost no one accepts.
It also implies that preventing flourishing people from existing carries no moral weight, contrary to widespread judgment.
Neartermism's appeal to intuitions about particular cases doesn't survive contact with intuitions about creation cases that pull the opposite way.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: There's a tradition of thought, going back centuries, that ethics is fundamentally about how we treat each other. The objects of moral concern are people in actual relation, not abstract welfare-quantities to be summed. When longtermism asks us to switch to an impersonal aggregating framework — caring about world-totals rather than relations — it's asking us to abandon what's been the central ethical insight of multiple traditions. That's a major philosophical move, not a clarification of premises everyone shares. The neartermist position doesn't require novel philosophical defense; it inherits a defensible tradition that longtermism wants to discard.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists frame the disagreement as if person-affecting reasoning were a quirky philosophical position they're disposing of. But person-affecting reasoning is closer to the mainstream of ethical thought across history than impersonal aggregation is. The aggregation framework is a relatively recent innovation associated with classical utilitarianism, and it's been criticized from within and outside utilitarianism for its counterintuitive implications. Treating it as the obvious framework that 'just produces' longtermism gets the philosophical history backwards.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Person-affecting reasoning is closer to the mainstream of ethical thought across history than impersonal aggregation.
Impersonal aggregation is a relatively recent innovation associated with classical utilitarianism, and has been criticized for counterintuitive implications since its development.
Longtermism's framing of impersonal aggregation as the 'obvious' default reverses the actual philosophical history.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: What I find compelling here is that the person-affecting view, when developed carefully, ends up either collapsing into the impersonal view or producing conclusions everyone rejects. Take any version of the view you like; either it has to count merely possible people in some way (in which case it's not really person-affecting anymore, just impersonal aggregation in disguise), or it has to deny moral significance to creating happy people (which contradicts considered judgment). The view doesn't have a stable middle ground. Faced with the choice between collapsing into impersonal reasoning and accepting wildly counterintuitive conclusions, the honest move is to embrace the impersonal view, which is what longtermism is.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists often invoke person-affecting intuitions as if they were a stable philosophical anchor. But the view doesn't have a stable form: every careful development either collapses back into impersonal aggregation or accepts conclusions widely rejected. The instability isn't a contingent flaw but a structural feature — person-affecting reasoning tries to make moral status depend on actual existence in a way that can't accommodate the obvious moral significance of creation choices. The neartermist position rests on a philosophical foundation that doesn't actually hold up under examination.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Every careful development of the person-affecting view either collapses into impersonal reasoning or accepts conclusions almost no one accepts.
The instability is structural, not contingent; the view tries to make moral status depend on actual existence in a way that can't accommodate creation choices.
Faced with the unstable middle, embracing the impersonal view (and longtermism) is the philosophically honest move.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Person-affecting reasoning has its difficulties — every philosophical view does — but the difficulties don't license the move to impersonal aggregation. The careful person-affecting traditions in philosophy have developed sophisticated responses to the standard objections. They acknowledge the puzzles around population ethics, the challenges of comparison cases, the strangeness of asymmetries — and they offer principled responses. Treating the view as if it were obviously broken, and impersonal aggregation as the obvious replacement, oversimplifies decades of philosophical work and underestimates what person-affecting frameworks can actually deliver.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists tend to characterize person-affecting reasoning as a position that either collapses into their view or produces absurdities. But this is dismissive of the actual philosophical literature, which has developed person-affecting frameworks of considerable subtlety. Narveson, Heyd, Roberts, and others have constructed views that handle the standard puzzles without collapsing into impersonal aggregation. Saying 'the view collapses or accepts absurdities' isn't a refutation of these views; it's a refusal to engage with them. The actual choice is between two developed traditions, not between a coherent view and a broken one.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: The careful philosophical literature on person-affecting views (Narveson, Heyd, Roberts, others) has developed sophisticated responses to standard objections.
Treating person-affecting reasoning as obviously broken oversimplifies decades of work in the tradition.
The actual philosophical disagreement is between two developed traditions, not between a coherent view and a broken one.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: I think the cleanest argument here is the comparison between two world-trajectories. World A: humanity continues, with ten billion flourishing people existing across the next several centuries. World B: humanity goes extinct now, with the present billion living out their natural lives but no one being created afterward. Almost everyone judges World A better than World B. But the person-affecting view has trouble explaining why. No one in World B is harmed by their non-existence; no one in World A is benefited by being created (since they didn't exist beforehand). The judgment that A is better requires comparing world-states impersonally, which is just impersonal aggregation. Once you've accepted that move, longtermism follows.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists try to handle the World A vs World B case from a person-affecting starting point, they have to do considerable philosophical work to get the intuitive answer. The simplest person-affecting view says A is no better than B, since no one in B is harmed. More sophisticated versions invent welfare-relations between possible and actual people, or appeal to wide preference-satisfaction across present generations. But these are repairs to a view that struggles with the case, not natural extensions of it. The simpler explanation — impersonal aggregation makes A better than B — is closer to the moral judgment.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Almost everyone judges a world with future flourishing populations better than one with extinction; this judgment requires impersonal comparison.
Person-affecting handlings of this case require philosophical work that wouldn't be needed under impersonal aggregation.
The simpler explanation — that we're committed to impersonal world-comparison — is closer to the moral judgment than the elaborate person-affecting alternatives.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The World A vs World B comparison is a classic case in population ethics, and person-affecting views have well-developed responses to it. One natural response: the wrongness of extinction isn't about a comparison between two world-states but about the present-tense significance of cutting off humanity's future, which is a value present people care about and have reason to preserve. This isn't impersonal aggregation in disguise; it's an account of why present people have reason to care about humanity's continuation, grounded in our own values and projects. The person-affecting view doesn't need impersonal world-comparison to recognize that extinction is bad.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists frame thought experiments like World A vs World B as if they unambiguously support impersonal aggregation. But the unambiguity is largely an artifact of how the cases are framed. Person-affecting views can recognize that present people have strong reasons to care about humanity's continuation — reasons grounded in present values, projects, and relationships, not in impersonal welfare-bookkeeping. This handles the case without committing to the impersonal framework. Longtermists tend to dismiss this handling as 'not really person-affecting,' but it's a natural development of the view, not a betrayal of it.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Person-affecting views can ground the wrongness of extinction in present-people's values and reasons rather than in impersonal world-comparison.
The 'present values' grounding isn't impersonal aggregation in disguise; it's a coherent person-affecting account.
World-comparison thought experiments seem unambiguous because they're framed in impersonal terms; person-affecting views handle the cases on their own terms.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: There's a famous argument in population ethics due to Parfit that I find compelling on this. Imagine you can either bring into existence Person A, who will live a flourishing life, or Person B, who will live a flourishing life of exactly the same kind. You can't bring both. The person-affecting view has trouble saying anything about this case — neither A nor B is benefited or harmed by the choice, since neither exists yet to be benefited or harmed. But intuitively, the choice between bringing A and bringing B is morally inconsequential, while the choice between bringing one of them and bringing neither is morally consequential. This pattern of judgments fits impersonal reasoning naturally and person-affecting reasoning awkwardly.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who appeal to person-affecting intuitions tend not to engage with the technical results in population ethics. The literature has been unkind to strict person-affecting views — Parfit's non-identity problem, the asymmetry between procreative ethics and welfare ethics, the various impossibility results. The careful work in the field has consistently shown that person-affecting reasoning doesn't have stable solutions to standard population-ethics puzzles. Invoking it as a philosophical anchor while ignoring this literature isn't really doing philosophy.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Parfit's non-identity problem and related results put substantial pressure on strict person-affecting views.
The technical literature in population ethics has consistently shown that person-affecting reasoning doesn't have stable solutions to standard puzzles.
Invoking person-affecting reasoning as a philosophical anchor without engaging this literature is selective.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The technical results in population ethics are real, but they don't settle the philosophical question in the way longtermists suggest. Yes, Parfit's puzzles are difficult; yes, every view in population ethics has uncomfortable cases. But this is true of impersonal aggregation too — the Repugnant Conclusion, sadistic conclusion, mere addition paradox, and various impossibility results affect aggregation views just as severely. Picking person-affecting views' difficulties as decisive while ignoring impersonal views' parallel difficulties is selective. Both traditions face puzzles; the disagreement isn't really about which has difficulties but about which puzzles bother you more.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke the technical results against person-affecting views, they tend to ignore the parallel results against impersonal aggregation. The Repugnant Conclusion is at least as troubling as the non-identity problem; the mere addition paradox is at least as challenging as person-affecting asymmetries. The technical literature isn't a one-way street that ends at impersonal aggregation; it's a landscape where every view has uncomfortable cases. Selectively citing the difficulties of one side while ignoring the parallel difficulties of the other is rhetorical, not analytical.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Impersonal aggregation faces parallel technical difficulties (Repugnant Conclusion, mere addition, sadistic conclusion) that longtermists tend to underweight.
The technical literature is a landscape where every view has uncomfortable cases, not a one-way street that ends at impersonal aggregation.
Selectively citing difficulties of person-affecting views while ignoring parallel difficulties of impersonal views is rhetorical, not analytical.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The deeper question here is what ethics is fundamentally about. The longtermist position, drawing on the impersonal tradition from Sidgwick to contemporary utilitarianism, is that ethics is about the impartial promotion of welfare wherever it occurs. The person-affecting position holds that ethics is about how we treat each other — specifically, the people we're related to in actual or future relation. Both positions have philosophical credentials, but the impersonal one has the advantage that it actually generates the conclusions we want about populations: that creating flourishing is good, that preventing flourishing is bad, that more conscious life is better than less. The person-affecting view struggles to deliver these standard judgments without invoking impersonal reasoning surreptitiously.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists defend person-affecting views, they often want to keep the conclusions of impersonal reasoning while rejecting the framework. They want to say creating flourishing is good (impersonal conclusion), but ground the goodness in some person-affecting consideration. They want to say extinction is bad (impersonal conclusion), but ground the badness in present-people's preferences. The pattern is consistent: keeping the impersonal-reasoning verdicts while denying the framework that delivers them. This selective use of conclusions is what makes the position unstable.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Impersonal aggregation generates the standard judgments we want about populations (creation is good, prevention is bad, more flourishing is better) directly.
Person-affecting views often have to invoke impersonal-style reasoning to deliver these standard judgments, which is unstable.
The pattern of keeping impersonal verdicts while rejecting the impersonal framework characterizes much careful person-affecting writing.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'what ethics is fundamentally about' question is genuinely contested, and the longtermist answer — impartial promotion of welfare — isn't the obvious answer it's sometimes presented as. There are deep traditions in ethics — virtue ethics, care ethics, contractualism — that don't reduce to welfare-aggregation. These traditions ground morality in the texture of human relation, in the kinds of people we should be, in agreements between rational beings. None of them is well-captured by 'impartial welfare promotion.' Longtermism's preferred framework is one tradition among several, not the inevitable answer to the question.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists tend to write as if the disagreement between impersonal aggregation and person-affecting views were the only relevant philosophical question. But there are deeper questions about what ethics is fundamentally about, and on these deeper questions there are well-developed traditions (virtue ethics, care ethics, contractualism) that don't reduce to welfare-aggregation at all. Person-affecting views connect more naturally to these traditions than impersonal aggregation does. The longtermist case implicitly assumes a particular metaethics — strong impartialist consequentialism — that's contested in ways the framework rarely acknowledges.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Multiple ethical traditions (virtue ethics, care ethics, contractualism) don't reduce to welfare-aggregation; longtermism's framework presupposes a particular metaethics.
Person-affecting views connect more naturally to these traditions than impersonal aggregation does.
The framework's implicit metaethics — strong impartialist consequentialism — is contested in ways longtermists rarely acknowledge.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The most direct way to test whether you accept person-affecting reasoning is to ask: does adding a flourishing life to a world make that world better, all else equal? If yes, you're committed to impersonal aggregation in some form, and longtermism follows when you take the principle seriously. If no — if you really think adding a happy person doesn't improve the world — you're committed to a position that conflicts sharply with most considered moral judgments. There aren't many places in ethics where the dialectical situation is this clean. The acceptance of impersonal reasoning is widely shared even when it's not explicitly endorsed; longtermism just makes it explicit.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists frequently want to deny that adding flourishing lives improves the world while still maintaining that, e.g., saving present lives is good. But the structure of these judgments is the same: in both cases, the world contains more flourishing afterward than it would have otherwise. Treating one as morally significant and the other as not requires a principled distinction, and the most natural distinction — that one involves harm-avoidance to determinate people and the other involves benefit-creation for non-determinate ones — turns out to be hard to defend. The asymmetry doesn't survive the question 'why is harm-avoidance privileged over benefit-creation in this way?'
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The question 'does adding a flourishing life improve the world?' is the simplest way to test commitment to impersonal reasoning.
Neartermists who say no to this question commit to conclusions that conflict with most considered moral judgments.
The asymmetry between harm-avoidance and benefit-creation that neartermism relies on is hard to defend principledly.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: There's a real asymmetry between harm and benefit, and the person-affecting view captures it where impersonal aggregation can't. The strong intuition that we have stronger reasons to avoid creating suffering than to create flourishing — that we have obligations not to bring miserable beings into existence but no obligation to bring happy ones — is widely shared and doesn't fit easily into impersonal aggregation. Person-affecting views handle the asymmetry naturally: harm requires a victim (which a person-affecting view can specify), while pure benefit-creation has no specific beneficiary (which a person-affecting view recognizes as a reason for weakened obligation). This isn't an unstable middle ground; it's a principled response to a real moral asymmetry.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists ask 'does adding a flourishing life improve the world?' they're presenting one half of an asymmetry as if it were the whole story. The corresponding question — 'does preventing a miserable life improve the world?' — gets answers that are typically much stronger. We feel strong reasons not to create suffering and weaker reasons (or no reasons) to create flourishing. Person-affecting views capture this asymmetry; impersonal aggregation has to either deny the asymmetry or invent ad-hoc machinery to handle it. The neartermist position is the one that fits the asymmetry naturally.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Strong asymmetry between harm and benefit (we have stronger obligations not to create suffering than to create flourishing) is widely shared and important.
Person-affecting views capture this asymmetry naturally; impersonal aggregation has to invent machinery or deny the asymmetry.
The 'add flourishing life' question, asked alone, hides the asymmetry that's actually at work in the moral psychology.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: I think the case here ultimately comes down to whether you think the impersonal good of the world matters at all. If you do — if you think the world is better when it contains more flourishing and less suffering, considered as a whole — then you're committed to impersonal reasoning, and longtermism follows when you take that reasoning seriously. The person-affecting view has to deny that the impersonal good of the world matters, or to redefine it so it can be cashed out in person-affecting terms. The first denial conflicts with widespread intuition; the second redefinition is unstable. Either way, the position is harder to maintain than it appears.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists tend to express person-affecting reasoning in cases where it produces the answer they want, and quietly switch to impersonal reasoning in cases where person-affecting reasoning would give the wrong answer. This selective use is what makes the position seem stable when examined locally and unstable when examined as a whole. A consistent person-affecting view either has to bite the bullets (deny that adding flourishing improves the world, deny that preventing extinction is intrinsically good) or to redefine impersonal reasoning as person-affecting in disguise. Both options have costs.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: If the impersonal good of the world matters at all, longtermism follows when you take that reasoning seriously across populations and time.
The person-affecting view has to either deny impersonal good or redefine it; both options have costs.
Selective use of person-affecting reasoning (where it gives wanted answers) plus impersonal reasoning (elsewhere) is what makes the position appear stable.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Person-affecting views aren't a denial that the world's impersonal good matters; they're an account of what that good consists in. On a careful person-affecting view, the world is better when it goes better for the people who are or will be in it. This isn't a denial of impersonal value; it's a specification of what impersonal value reduces to. The longtermist alternative, on which the world's good is some abstract welfare-quantity that floats free of any actual people's welfare, is a more exotic philosophical commitment than longtermists usually acknowledge. The person-affecting view isn't denying impersonal value; it's offering a more grounded account of it.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists frame the choice as 'either accept impersonal value or deny that the world's good matters,' they're presenting a false dichotomy. Person-affecting views can affirm that the world's good matters while specifying what that good consists in. The world is better when it goes better for the people in it; that's a recognizable account of impersonal value, not a denial of it. The longtermist insistence on disconnecting impersonal value from actual people's welfare is the philosophically exotic move, and it's the move that needs defending — not the more grounded person-affecting alternative.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Person-affecting views can specify impersonal value as 'going better for the people who are or will be in the world,' without denying that impersonal value matters.
The longtermist alternative — impersonal value disconnected from actual people's welfare — is the more exotic philosophical commitment.
Framing the disagreement as 'accept impersonal value or deny it' is a false dichotomy that obscures person-affecting alternatives.

career_choice.theme: What kind of work a person aiming to do the most good should pursue — civilizational-trajectory work or concrete near-term interventions.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Someone trying to do the most good with their career should be working on civilization-scale questions — AI safety, biosecurity, pandemic prevention, governance of powerful technologies. The leverage is enormous: a career spent reducing the probability of civilizational catastrophe affects the welfare of orders of magnitude more people than any near-term intervention can. Direct harm-reduction work is good and meaningful, but on the scale of expected impact, trajectory-shaping work simply wins, and the people who do this calculation honestly tend to land on it.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The 'concrete present harm is more important than speculative future work' argument confuses tractability with importance. Yes, it's easier to point to a child saved by a malaria net than to a civilization saved by AI governance work. But that's an artifact of measurement, not of moral significance. The ease of pointing at outcomes shouldn't drive the moral calculation; the magnitude of outcomes should. And on magnitude, trajectory work dominates.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The expected-value calculation, even with very conservative numbers, favors trajectory work over near-term interventions by orders of magnitude.
Concrete near-term interventions have diminishing returns and many smart people working on them; trajectory work has higher counterfactual impact.
Most of what the strongest direct-impact careers achieve is a small fraction of what trajectory-shaping work could achieve if it succeeds.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Someone trying to do the most good should work on concrete near-term harms — global poverty, preventable disease, mental health, education — where the impact on real people is measurable and the chain of causation is short. Trajectory-shaping careers depend on long chains of speculation: that the work matters at all, that the individual contribution moves probabilities, that the predicted catastrophes are the right ones. Each link introduces uncertainty, and the product is much weaker than the longtermist framing suggests. Direct, well-evidenced impact is more morally compelling than speculative high-leverage work.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist career argument depends on multiplying probabilities and population estimates that no one can actually defend. 'Astronomical expected value' is a calculation that treats deep uncertainty as if it were well-quantified; in any other domain we'd recognize this as overconfidence. Direct work on present harms doesn't require these inflated calculations; it requires evidence that the intervention helps real people, which is achievable and measurable in ways longtermist work isn't.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Direct interventions on present harms have measurable, evidence-based impact; trajectory work depends on speculative chains of causation.
The 'expected value' calculations longtermism relies on multiply weakly-grounded estimates; the result is not a serious calculation.
Real people helped now is morally weightier than speculative populations possibly affected through long causal chains.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The career question is fundamentally about leverage. Some careers reduce immediate suffering — important work, but bounded by how many people one career can directly help. Other careers shape institutions, technologies, or risks that affect the trajectory of civilization itself. The latter has dramatically more leverage when it succeeds, and even modest probabilities of success make the expected impact much larger. A person trying to do the most good should be biased toward high-leverage work, and trajectory-shaping careers are where the leverage actually lies.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists tend to undersell the leverage difference between direct harm-reduction and civilizational work. They acknowledge it abstractly but treat it as if it were a small factor in the calculation, when actually it's the dominant factor. A career that reduces existential risk by even tiny amounts has expected impact orders of magnitude beyond a career that directly helps thousands of people. The neartermist framing makes both kinds of work look comparable, but the underlying numbers don't support that.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Trajectory-shaping work has dramatically higher leverage than direct harm-reduction when it succeeds.
Even modest probabilities of success on high-leverage work produce expected impact much larger than direct work.
Neartermist comparisons systematically underweight the leverage difference between work types.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The leverage argument for longtermist careers depends on a particular accounting where 'expected impact' is calculated by multiplying speculative probabilities by speculative magnitudes. Real leverage requires that the leverage actually exist — that the work actually moves the variables it claims to move. Most claimed trajectory-shaping work has weak evidence for its actual leverage on civilizational outcomes. Direct work on present harms has strong evidence for its leverage on the things it claims to address. The honest comparison gives a very different picture than the longtermist framing.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke leverage, they assume the leverage exists in the work they're recommending. But leverage isn't asserted into existence by claiming a career affects civilizational trajectories; it has to be evidenced. Most longtermist career recommendations have thin evidence that the work actually moves the variables it claims to move. Calling it 'high-leverage' on the basis of speculative impact pathways is leverage by stipulation, not leverage by demonstration. The neartermist alternative is leverage by demonstration: work whose leverage is visible in evidence.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Real leverage requires demonstrated impact on the variables a career claims to affect; longtermist work mostly hasn't demonstrated this.
Direct work on present harms has demonstrated leverage; trajectory work has stipulated leverage.
The leverage argument for longtermist careers assumes its conclusion (that the work has leverage) rather than evidencing it.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: What matters for career impact isn't just the absolute good done but the counterfactual — what would have happened without you. Direct harm-reduction work has many smart people in it, well-funded organizations, established interventions. Adding one more person, however talented, has limited counterfactual impact because the work would mostly happen anyway. Trajectory-shaping work is much more talent-constrained: relatively few people have the skills to do AI safety research, biosecurity policy, or alignment work, and the work that needs doing exceeds the people doing it. Adding talent to this work has dramatically larger counterfactual impact.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The neartermist career argument tends to ignore counterfactual impact entirely. It compares the magnitude of a single career's direct effect on present people to the magnitude of speculative trajectory effects, and concludes that the direct work wins. But this misses that the direct work would mostly be done anyway — the field is funded, the talent pool is deep, the methods are established. Trajectory work has a much smaller talent pool and clearer marginal need. Counterfactual impact, properly considered, often favors trajectory work even when total impact comparisons don't.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Direct harm-reduction has deep talent pools and established infrastructure; counterfactual impact of adding one person is correspondingly limited.
Trajectory work is talent-constrained; counterfactual impact of adding capable people is high.
Comparing total impact ignores counterfactual; properly considered, counterfactual impact favors trajectory work.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The counterfactual-impact argument for trajectory careers cuts both ways. Yes, direct harm-reduction has many people working on it. But also: trajectory work has many people working on it relative to its actual demonstrated impact. The number of people in AI safety, longtermist philanthropy, and adjacent fields has grown substantially in recent years, while the demonstrated impact of this work on actual civilizational outcomes remains weak. Adding more people to a field whose impact is unclear isn't obviously a higher-leverage move than adding to fields with demonstrated impact.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists invoke counterfactual impact as if trajectory work were uniquely talent-constrained. But the actual ratio of people-to-demonstrated-impact in longtermist fields is comparable to or worse than direct harm-reduction. AI safety has many researchers; biosecurity has substantial funding; longtermist philanthropy has organized infrastructure. The 'we need more people' framing has been a feature of these fields for a decade now, while concrete civilizational-impact remains hard to demonstrate. Counterfactual impact requires actual impact to be counterfactual against, and the actual impact is the question.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Trajectory work has substantial people and funding; the 'talent-constrained' framing is overstated.
Counterfactual impact requires demonstrated impact to be counterfactual against; trajectory work's impact is mostly speculative.
Adding people to fields with unclear impact isn't obviously higher-leverage than adding to fields with clear impact.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: If you think carefully about what a single person can do over a career — call it 80,000 hours of working life — the comparison between high-impact paths makes the longtermist conclusion almost forced. The variation in impact between different careers is enormous; the difference between a typical career and an exceptionally good one is much larger than the difference between, say, two typical careers. When you do the calculation honestly, the careers that come out on top are mostly trajectory-shaping ones: AI safety, biosecurity, longtermist research, work on civilizational governance. This isn't because direct work is bad; it's because the variance in impact strongly favors high-leverage work, and high-leverage work is mostly trajectory work.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The neartermist response — 'but trajectory work is too speculative' — is exactly what the careful comparison undercuts. Even discounting heavily for speculative impact, trajectory work's expected value remains enormous because the upside is so large. Refusing to consider speculative-but-high-impact careers means ignoring the careers where most of the impact actually lies. This isn't being careful; it's being systematically biased toward measurable mediocrity over high-variance excellence.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Variance in career impact is enormous; high-impact careers are dramatically better than typical ones.
When you compare careers honestly, trajectory-shaping work consistently appears at the top.
Refusing to consider speculative-high-impact work systematically biases toward measurable but lower-impact careers.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'careful career calculation' that produces longtermist recommendations is largely doing what the assumptions told it to do. If you assume that civilizational catastrophe is reasonably probable, that trajectory work meaningfully reduces this probability, and that future populations are vast, the calculation produces the longtermist answer. None of these assumptions is well-grounded. The calculation isn't actually showing that trajectory work has higher expected value; it's showing that under particular assumptions, it would. Honest career advice would acknowledge the dependence on assumptions rather than presenting the conclusion as if it followed from neutral calculation.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist career-calculation framework presents itself as neutral expected-value reasoning, but the inputs are loaded.
