Calling longtermist guesses 'credences' borrows decision-theory rigor-language without meeting the verification standards that justify it.
Expected-value-with-credences reasoning is rigorous when credences are calibrated; the framework's credences aren't.

expected_value_framework.theme: Whether expected-value reasoning is the right framework for ethics under uncertainty, especially when very large numbers are involved.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Expected-value reasoning is the right framework for ethical decisions under uncertainty, even — especially — when very large numbers are involved. The alternative is some form of 'don't trust the math when it produces uncomfortable conclusions,' which is just confirmation bias dressed up as humility. If you accept that probabilities and outcomes can be combined in everyday decision-making, the same combination has to apply at larger scales. Refusing to multiply probability by magnitude when the magnitudes are large is an arbitrary exception that isn't principled.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists often want to suspend expected-value reasoning specifically when it produces longtermist conclusions, while accepting it everywhere else. This is unprincipled. Either expected-value reasoning is the right framework for decisions under uncertainty or it isn't, and you don't get to switch frameworks based on whether you like the answer. The 'Pascalian mugging' framing is meant to make the longtermist conclusion look like a mathematical trick, but the structure isn't a trick; it's just consistent application of the rule everyone uses elsewhere.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Expected-value reasoning is the standard framework for decisions under uncertainty; suspending it specifically when it produces longtermist conclusions is unprincipled.
The 'numbers don't apply at large scale' move is an arbitrary exception, not a defended philosophical position.
Probability times magnitude is what every other decision domain uses; ethics shouldn't get a free pass from this.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Expected-value reasoning breaks down at the scales longtermism asks us to apply it to. When you're multiplying tiny probabilities by astronomical magnitudes, the result is dominated by the magnitudes, and the magnitudes are exactly what we're least confident about. The framework gives a false sense of rigor: it produces a number, but the number reflects the assumptions you put in more than it reflects anything about the world. 'Pascalian' arguments — where any low-probability claim about huge stakes dominates the calculation — show what's wrong with applying expected-value reasoning beyond its useful range.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist defense of expected-value reasoning treats it as a context-free principle of rationality, but it's actually a tool that works in specific conditions: well-characterized probabilities, well-understood outcomes, repeated decisions where errors average out. None of these conditions hold for longtermist calculations, which means the tool isn't the right one for the job. Insisting on it anyway, and treating critics as 'innumerate,' confuses tool-fitness with rationality.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Expected-value reasoning works in conditions of well-characterized probabilities and repeated decisions; longtermist applications meet neither condition.
Pascalian-mugging structures show the framework breaks down at extremes; longtermism applies it precisely at those extremes.
The number that comes out of expected-value calculation reflects the assumptions put in; for longtermist calculations, the assumptions dominate.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The right way to think about expected-value reasoning is that it's the disciplined version of what everyone does informally. When you decide whether to wear a seatbelt, you're implicitly multiplying probability of accident by magnitude of harm and concluding it's worth the small inconvenience. When you buy insurance, same structure. When you save for retirement, same structure. Longtermism just extends this disciplined reasoning to civilizational-scale stakes. The math doesn't change because the stakes are larger; it just produces conclusions that may be uncomfortable. Discomfort with conclusions isn't a refutation of methodology.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who reject longtermist EV calculations as 'just multiplying probabilities by magnitudes' don't usually reject the same operation when it produces conclusions they're comfortable with. The structure of the reasoning is the same in seatbelt-wearing, insurance-buying, and longtermist intervention-recommendation. Selective rejection of the framework when it produces uncomfortable conclusions is what's at stake; the framework itself is well-established.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Expected-value reasoning underlies routine decisions (seatbelts, insurance, savings); it's not an exotic framework.
The structure of EV reasoning doesn't change with the scale of stakes; only the magnitudes do.
Selective rejection when EV produces uncomfortable conclusions is what's at issue, not the framework's general validity.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Expected-value reasoning works for everyday decisions because the probabilities are roughly known, the outcomes are bounded, and we have feedback loops to adjust. None of these conditions hold for civilizational-scale interventions. We don't have known probabilities for AI risk, we don't have bounded outcomes for civilizational catastrophe, and we don't have feedback loops to verify our calculations. Applying EV reasoning to these cases is using a tool outside its operating range. The tool produces numbers; the numbers don't necessarily mean what we want them to mean.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke seatbelt-wearing and insurance-buying as precedents for EV reasoning at civilizational scale, they're conflating cases where the framework works (known probabilities, bounded outcomes, feedback loops) with cases where it doesn't (unknown probabilities, unbounded outcomes, no feedback). The methodology that works in everyday cases doesn't transfer cleanly to civilizational cases. Citing the everyday cases as license for the civilizational ones is selective.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: EV reasoning in everyday decisions works because probabilities are known, outcomes are bounded, and feedback loops exist.
Civilizational-scale interventions lack all three conditions; the methodology doesn't transfer cleanly.
Citing everyday EV cases as license for civilizational EV cases is selective use of methodology.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The 'Pascalian mugging' objection to expected-value reasoning has a specific scope. It applies when probabilities are vanishingly small and stakes are arbitrarily large, in cases where the structure can be applied to any low-probability claim with sufficient framing. Longtermist interventions don't have this structure. The probabilities involved aren't vanishingly small (estimates are in the percent range, not the trillionths range), the stakes are bounded (civilization, not infinite multiverses), and the calculations are constrained by what we actually know about specific risks. Calling longtermism Pascalian conflates two different argument structures.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists deploy the 'Pascalian mugging' label to dismiss longtermist EV calculations, but the analogy is loose. Pascalian arguments require infinitesimal probabilities and infinite stakes; longtermism uses moderate probabilities and finite (if very large) stakes. The structures are different in ways that matter for whether the standard Pascalian critiques apply. Borrowing the label without arguing the analogy is rhetorical; the actual question is whether longtermist EV calculations have the features that make Pascalian arguments problematic, and they mostly don't.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Pascalian arguments require infinitesimal probabilities and infinite stakes; longtermism uses moderate probabilities and finite stakes.
The Pascalian structure can be applied to any low-probability claim with sufficient framing; longtermist calculations are constrained by specific risk knowledge.
Borrowing the Pascalian label without arguing the analogy is rhetorical, not analytical.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The argument that longtermism isn't Pascalian relies on its probabilities being 'moderate' (in the percent range) and its stakes being 'finite' (civilization-scale). But these descriptions are themselves contested. Where do the percent-range probability estimates come from? Mostly from communities that take the topic seriously, with no track record for calibration. Where does 'civilization-scale' end? At trillions of future people, which from a present-tense perspective is functionally unbounded. The disanalogy with Pascalian arguments is weaker than longtermists suggest, because the probability estimates aren't actually grounded and the stakes aren't actually bounded in the relevant sense.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists distinguish their EV calculations from Pascalian arguments by claiming moderate probabilities and finite stakes. But 'moderate probabilities' that come from uncalibrated estimates by selected communities aren't really moderate in the relevant sense — they could be off by orders of magnitude. 'Finite stakes' at the trillions-of-future-people scale are functionally unbounded relative to anything we can verify. The Pascalian-mugging objection lands more cleanly than the disanalogy claim suggests.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: 'Moderate probabilities' for longtermist calculations come from uncalibrated estimates that could be off by orders of magnitude.
'Finite stakes' at civilizational scale are functionally unbounded relative to verifiable outcomes.
The disanalogy with Pascalian arguments is weaker than longtermists suggest because probability estimates aren't grounded and stakes aren't bounded in the relevant sense.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Reasonable disagreement about expected values doesn't undermine the EV framework; it just means the inputs are uncertain. The framework itself is sound: when probabilities and magnitudes can be estimated, multiplying them is what produces calibrated decision-making. Longtermism's contribution isn't a novel framework; it's careful application of standard EV reasoning to civilizational-scale stakes. Critics who disagree with specific EV calculations should engage with the inputs, not the framework. Disputing 'AI risk has 10% probability of catastrophe by 2100' is engaging with inputs; disputing 'EV reasoning shouldn't apply to civilizational cases' is disputing the framework on grounds that don't apply.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists tend to argue against specific longtermist EV calculations by attacking the framework, when their actual disagreement is with specific inputs. If you think 'AI risk has 10% probability' is wrong, the response is to argue for a different probability, not to argue that EV reasoning doesn't apply. By attacking the framework instead of the inputs, neartermists give the impression that they're rejecting longtermism on principled grounds when they're actually rejecting specific empirical claims while presenting the rejection as methodological.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Disagreement with specific EV calculations is disagreement with inputs; the framework itself is sound.
Engaging with inputs (probability estimates, magnitude estimates) is the appropriate way to push back on EV calculations.
Attacking the framework when the actual disagreement is with inputs is methodological misdirection.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'attack the inputs not the framework' move misses what's actually wrong with longtermist EV calculations. The problem isn't that we disagree about specific probability estimates; it's that the estimates aren't well-grounded enough to ground EV reasoning at all. EV reasoning requires inputs with some level of empirical grounding; longtermist inputs are mostly educated guesses by people whose calibration on these questions can't be measured. Engaging with the inputs as if they were calibrated estimates concedes the methodological point that's actually at stake.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists frame the disagreement as input-vs-framework, suggesting that legitimate critique should engage with their probability estimates. But this assumes the estimates are calibrated enough to be engaged with, which is exactly what's at issue. If the estimates are educated guesses by uncalibrated communities, treating them as inputs to EV calculations is the methodological problem. The 'engage with inputs' framing tries to enforce an analytical position that concedes the central methodological question.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: EV reasoning requires inputs with empirical grounding; longtermist inputs are mostly educated guesses without calibration.
Engaging with longtermist inputs as if they were calibrated estimates concedes the methodological point.
The 'attack inputs not framework' move enforces an analytical position that the methodology question is settled when it isn't.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The fundamental issue with rejecting EV reasoning at civilizational scale is that the alternative isn't well-defined. If you don't multiply probability by magnitude, what do you do? You can't do nothing — you still have to make decisions about resource allocation, intervention priority, governance design. So you're using some implicit weighting of probability and magnitude, just not making it explicit. The implicit weighting is usually less rigorous than the explicit one, more vulnerable to bias, and harder to evaluate. Insisting on rejecting EV calculation in these cases means insisting on a less disciplined alternative without naming what it is.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who reject EV reasoning for civilizational decisions usually don't replace it with anything specific; they replace it with intuition or unspecified judgment. But intuition and unspecified judgment have their own well-known problems: they're shaped by availability heuristic, status quo bias, identifiable-victim effects. EV reasoning isn't perfect, but the alternative the neartermist is implicitly proposing is worse, not better. The argument 'don't use EV at civilizational scale' is incomplete without specifying what to use instead, and the specifications usually fall apart on examination.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The alternative to EV reasoning isn't doing nothing; it's some implicit weighting that's usually less rigorous.
Intuition and unspecified judgment have known biases (availability, status quo, identifiable-victim effects).
Rejecting EV reasoning without specifying the alternative is incomplete; the alternatives usually fall apart on examination.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'what's the alternative' challenge to neartermist methodology is itself rigged. The alternative to bad EV reasoning isn't necessarily good EV reasoning; it can be 'use EV where it works and fall back on humbler heuristics where it doesn't.' These humbler heuristics — anchor in evidence-grounded interventions, attend to documented harms, work where causal mechanisms are clear — aren't perfect, but they're appropriate to conditions where EV reasoning isn't reliable. The challenge to specify a fully developed alternative methodology assumes that all decision-making must be methodologically uniform, which it doesn't.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists challenge neartermists to specify an alternative to EV reasoning, they're enforcing a uniformity assumption: that one methodology must apply everywhere. But decision-making isn't methodologically uniform. EV reasoning works in some conditions and not others; humbler heuristics work in some conditions and not others. The neartermist position isn't 'reject EV reasoning entirely' but 'recognize where EV reasoning is reliable and use other methods where it isn't.' The challenge to specify a single alternative methodology misframes the disagreement.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Decision-making isn't methodologically uniform; different conditions call for different methods.
The neartermist position isn't 'reject EV entirely' but 'recognize where it's reliable and use other methods where it isn't.'
Challenges to specify a single alternative methodology misframe the disagreement.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The Pascalian-mugging worry, properly understood, applies to specific argument structures, not to longtermist reasoning generally. The key feature of Pascalian arguments is that they can be constructed for any low-probability claim with sufficient framing — making them vulnerable to manipulation by anyone who can spin a sufficiently dramatic scenario. Longtermist EV calculations don't have this feature: they're constrained by specific risk-domains (AI, biosecurity, nuclear) with documented mechanisms, not freely constructable from arbitrary scenarios. The structural difference matters: Pascalian arguments are vulnerable to manipulation; constrained EV calculations aren't.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists invoke Pascalian-mugging worries as if all low-probability-high-stakes calculations were equally problematic. But the worries apply to argument structures that can be constructed freely from any sufficiently dramatic claim, and longtermist calculations don't have this feature. They're tied to specific documented risks with specific mechanisms. Treating longtermist calculations as vulnerable to the Pascalian critique requires ignoring how the calculations are actually constrained by the underlying risk domains.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Pascalian arguments are vulnerable to manipulation because they can be constructed for any low-probability claim; longtermist calculations are constrained by specific risk domains.
The structural difference between freely-constructable Pascalian arguments and constrained longtermist calculations matters for whether the critique applies.
Treating longtermist calculations as Pascalian requires ignoring the constraint by underlying documented risks.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'longtermist calculations are constrained by documented risks' defense relies on the documented-risks claim being well-grounded. But the relevant 'documentation' for longtermist risks is mostly philosophical argument and community consensus, not the kind of empirical grounding that constrains EV calculations in better-established domains. AI alignment risk is documented in the sense that some communities take it seriously; it's not documented in the sense that climate risk or pandemic risk is. The constraint that longtermists invoke to distinguish their reasoning from Pascalian arguments isn't actually doing the constraining work it claims.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists distinguish their EV calculations from Pascalian arguments by invoking 'documented risks,' they're using a weak sense of 'documented.' Climate risk is documented through physics and observation. Pandemic risk is documented through historical records and biology. AI alignment risk and similar longtermist concerns are documented through philosophical argument and community consensus. These are different kinds of documentation, and the longtermist defense of EV reasoning depends on conflating them.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Climate and pandemic risks are documented through physics, observation, and historical records.
Longtermist risks are documented through philosophical argument and community consensus, which is a much weaker sense of 'documented.'
The longtermist distinction between Pascalian arguments and their own calculations depends on conflating these senses of documentation.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Critics of longtermist EV reasoning sometimes argue that it produces 'fanatical' conclusions — that we should redirect huge resources to interventions whose expected value is dominated by tiny probabilities of huge effects. But fanaticism isn't a property of EV reasoning; it's a property of specific calculations with specific inputs. If your inputs include very small probabilities of very large effects, the calculation will produce dominance by those terms — and that's correct decision-making under those inputs. The complaint isn't really about EV reasoning; it's about the discomfort of acting on the calculations. The discomfort is real but doesn't refute the math.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists call longtermist EV conclusions 'fanatical,' they're using rhetoric to substitute for argument. The label is meant to make the conclusions sound unhinged without engaging with whether the underlying reasoning is sound. But the conclusions follow from specific premises about probabilities and magnitudes; if the premises are right, the conclusions are right. Calling them 'fanatical' doesn't address whether the premises are right. It just expresses discomfort with where the math leads.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: 'Fanaticism' is a property of specific calculations with specific inputs, not of EV reasoning itself.
If inputs include small probabilities of large effects, the calculation correctly shows dominance by those terms.
The 'fanatical' label substitutes rhetoric for argument; the actual question is whether the inputs are right.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'fanaticism' critique of EV reasoning isn't just rhetoric. It points at a real methodological feature: when expected-value calculations are dominated by terms involving small probabilities of huge effects, the calculations become unstable in ways that warrant caution. This isn't about emotional discomfort; it's about decision-theoretic robustness. Decisions whose entire justification rests on tiny probability terms are vulnerable to small errors in those probability estimates, in ways that decisions grounded in larger probabilities aren't. The critique tracks something real about when EV reasoning becomes unreliable.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists dismiss the fanaticism critique as rhetoric, but it tracks a real decision-theoretic concern. When EV calculations are dominated by tiny-probability-times-huge-magnitude terms, small errors in the probability estimates produce huge swings in the calculated expected value. This makes the calculations unstable in a way that decisions grounded in larger probabilities aren't. The instability is a methodological feature, not just a feeling, and it justifies caution about acting on EV calculations dominated by these terms.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: EV calculations dominated by tiny-probability-times-huge-magnitude terms are unstable to small errors in probability estimates.
This instability is a real decision-theoretic feature, not just emotional discomfort.
The 'fanaticism' critique tracks something real about when EV reasoning becomes unreliable.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Take a concrete case. Suppose you have $10 million to allocate. Option A: a near-term intervention with high confidence of helping a specific number of present people. Option B: a speculative trajectory-shaping intervention with low confidence of meaningfully reducing civilizational risk. If you actually run the EV calculation with reasonable inputs — even quite conservative ones — Option B often comes out ahead because civilizational risk affects so many possible future people. This isn't a freak result; it's what consistent application of EV reasoning produces at these scales. Refusing the conclusion requires either rejecting EV reasoning (which is unprincipled if you accept it elsewhere) or rejecting the specific inputs (which is a different kind of disagreement).
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists reject the standard $10M allocation example, they typically do so by either disputing the inputs (which is fair but a different kind of argument) or by gesturing at 'something must be wrong' with the calculation. The 'something must be wrong' move is what's at issue. Either the calculation is correct (in which case neartermism is wrong) or specific inputs are wrong (in which case the disagreement is empirical). 'The conclusion can't be right because it feels wrong' isn't an argument; it's a refusal of the conclusion.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Concrete EV calculations on resource-allocation decisions consistently favor longtermist options when run with reasonable inputs.
Refusing the conclusion requires either rejecting EV reasoning (unprincipled) or rejecting specific inputs (empirical disagreement).
'The conclusion feels wrong' isn't an argument against EV reasoning; it's a refusal to accept where the math leads.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The standard $10M-allocation example is run with inputs that pre-determine the outcome. If you assume civilizational risk is real, that the intervention reduces it by some amount, and that future populations are vast, the calculation produces longtermist dominance. But these assumptions are exactly what's at issue. Building a calculation on assumptions that load it toward your conclusion, then claiming the conclusion follows from the math, is putting the conclusion in the premise. The math is downstream of the assumptions; the assumptions are where the actual disagreement lives.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists run the $10M-allocation example, they're using inputs that contain the conclusion. Civilizational risk is real (assumption), interventions reduce it (assumption), future populations are vast (assumption). The calculation just multiplies these together and produces dominance. But the assumptions are the contested part. Presenting the calculation as if it followed from neutral math obscures that the math is downstream of substantial empirical commitments that aren't well-grounded.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Standard EV examples use inputs that contain the conclusion (civilizational risk real, interventions effective, populations vast).
Calculations downstream of contested assumptions inherit the contestedness; the math doesn't make the assumptions neutral.
Presenting EV calculations as if they followed from neutral math obscures the substantial empirical commitments embedded in the inputs.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The criticism that longtermist EV calculations 'multiply weakly-grounded numbers' applies to many forms of decision-making under uncertainty, not just longtermism. Climate policy, pandemic preparedness, financial regulation, military planning all involve multiplying uncertain estimates of probabilities and magnitudes. The fact that the inputs are uncertain doesn't invalidate the framework; it just means the conclusions come with appropriate uncertainty. Longtermism doesn't require certainty in its inputs; it requires that the inputs be reasonable estimates with reasonable uncertainty bounds. That's a much weaker requirement than the critique suggests.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who reject longtermist EV calculations on grounds of input uncertainty would, applied consistently, have to reject most policy-relevant uncertainty calculations: climate models, financial risk assessments, pandemic projections. These all 'multiply weakly-grounded numbers.' The neartermist position usually doesn't reject these — it accepts them. So the rejection of longtermist calculations isn't really about the multiplication of uncertain inputs; it's about something else (probably the magnitude of stakes or the speculativeness of the underlying claims), but the explicit objection is misdirected.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Climate policy, financial regulation, and pandemic preparedness all involve multiplying uncertain inputs; the practice is widespread.
Neartermist rejection of longtermism on input-uncertainty grounds would reject these accepted uncertainty calculations if applied consistently.
The actual objection isn't about uncertain inputs; it's about something else (magnitude or speculativeness), but the framing misses this.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Climate models and pandemic projections multiply uncertain inputs, yes — but the inputs have grounding that longtermist inputs don't. Climate models are validated against historical data and physical mechanisms. Pandemic projections are validated against historical pandemic patterns and biological mechanisms. The 'uncertain inputs' in these cases come with track-record-based confidence intervals. Longtermist inputs come with whatever the relevant community happens to estimate, without comparable validation. The comparison treats different kinds of uncertainty as equivalent.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke climate models and pandemic projections as precedents for multiplying uncertain inputs, they're conflating validated uncertainty (track-record-based, mechanism-grounded) with unvalidated uncertainty (community-consensus-based, mechanism-light). The methodology of multiplying uncertain inputs works in the first case because the uncertainty is calibrated; in the second case it doesn't, because there's no calibration. The precedent doesn't transfer cleanly.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Climate and pandemic models have track-record-based confidence intervals; longtermist inputs don't.
Validated uncertainty (mechanism-grounded) is different from unvalidated uncertainty (community-consensus-based).
The methodology of multiplying uncertain inputs works in calibrated cases; the longtermist precedent doesn't transfer.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: I think the cleanest defense of EV reasoning at civilizational scale is that the alternative — refusing to apply quantitative reasoning to large-stakes decisions — has worse failure modes. Without quantitative reasoning, you fall back on intuitions, narratives, and heuristics that are systematically biased: identifiable-victim effects, scope insensitivity, status quo bias, recency. EV reasoning, even with uncertain inputs, gives you a structure to think about these decisions that's at least more transparent than the alternatives. You can argue with the inputs; you can update on evidence; you can compare across cases. That's much harder to do with intuition-driven decision-making.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who reject EV reasoning at civilizational scale don't usually have a developed alternative — they fall back on intuitions and heuristics that have known biases. EV reasoning isn't perfect, but it's transparent in a way that intuition isn't, and that transparency is itself a methodological advantage. You can disagree with EV calculations explicitly, identify which inputs you dispute, and trace through the implications. Disagreeing with intuition-driven judgments is much harder, because the reasoning isn't accessible. The neartermist preference for less-quantitative methods sacrifices a real methodological good.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Quantitative EV reasoning is transparent in a way intuition-driven reasoning isn't; you can argue with inputs explicitly.
Intuition-driven decision-making has known biases (identifiable victim, scope insensitivity, status quo, recency).
Neartermist preference for less-quantitative methods sacrifices methodological transparency.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The argument 'EV reasoning is at least transparent' assumes that the EV calculation is transparent — but at civilizational scale, the calculation's transparency is an illusion. The numbers look transparent (probability times magnitude), but where do the numbers come from? Educated guesses. Whose guesses? People in particular communities. With what calibration? None. The 'transparency' that EV reasoning is supposed to provide depends on the inputs being verifiable; for civilizational-scale reasoning, they're not. So the argument that EV is more transparent than intuition collapses: in conditions where calibration isn't possible, EV reasoning is just intuition with a multiplication step.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists defend EV reasoning by appealing to its transparency, they're describing how the framework works in ideal conditions, not how it works in their actual applications. Transparency requires verifiable inputs; civilizational-scale EV inputs aren't verifiable. So what looks like transparent quantitative reasoning is actually intuition-with-numbers — the same kind of reasoning the framework is supposed to improve on, just dressed up. The transparency advantage is largely lost in the conditions where longtermism actually applies the framework.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: EV reasoning's transparency advantage requires verifiable inputs; civilizational-scale inputs aren't verifiable.
Without verifiable inputs, EV reasoning is intuition-with-numbers — the kind of reasoning it's supposed to improve on.
The transparency advantage is largely lost in the conditions where longtermism actually applies EV reasoning.

present_injustice.theme: Whether longtermist priorities risk neglecting present injustice, and whether this is a feature or a bug of the framework.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Longtermism doesn't entail neglecting present injustice; it entails recalibrating how present injustice fits into the larger moral picture. Many present injustices are themselves long-term issues — civilizational stability, the political conditions for trust, the distribution of AI development authority. Working on these is both longtermist and present-justice-attentive. The framing that pits longtermism against present justice is mostly a misunderstanding: you can take long-term considerations seriously without dismissing immediate harms, and most longtermists do.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The 'longtermism neglects present injustice' charge is rhetorically powerful but mostly empirically wrong. Longtermist organizations fund global health, work on international governance, support refugee crises. The charge sticks when longtermism is presented as a either/or, but the actual practice is a portfolio approach where present and long-term considerations both feature. Neartermists who frame longtermism as necessarily neglectful are arguing against a strawman that doesn't match the actual movement.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Many present injustices are themselves long-term issues (institutional, political, technological); longtermist work often addresses them.
Longtermist organizations and individuals in practice fund a portfolio that includes present-tense work, not just speculative trajectory work.
The trade-off framing is not the only option; serious moral reasoning can hold both kinds of considerations together.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Longtermism in practice systematically diverts attention and resources from present injustice. The framework treats huge present harms — global poverty, ongoing violence, structural injustice — as comparatively small next to speculative future welfare, and the resource allocation follows. This is visible in how longtermist organizations actually spend money, who they hire, what research they fund. The defense that 'longtermism doesn't entail neglect' may be technically true, but it's beside the point: in practice, the framework produces neglect, and that's a serious moral cost.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists protest that they don't neglect present injustice, but the protestations are weaker than the actual allocations. When EV calculations consistently say 'speculative future work has astronomical value' and present injustice doesn't, the framework is structurally biased against the present, even if individual longtermists temper this with personal discretion. The bias is in the framework, and the framework determines the resource allocation in the long run, not individual softening.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Resource allocation patterns of longtermist-aligned philanthropy and institutions skew systematically toward speculative work and away from present harms.
The framework's structural bias against present harms isn't fully neutralized by individual longtermists' moderation.
Present injustice is morally urgent in ways that the longtermist calculation systematically underweights; the urgency is what the framework loses sight of.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The strongest longtermist work is continuous with present-justice work, not opposed to it. Concern about civilization-scale risks isn't separable from concern about who gets harmed by them: pandemics hit poor populations harder, AI development is concentrated in wealthy countries, climate effects fall disproportionately on the global south. Longtermist analysis of these risks naturally includes attention to how harms are distributed, and longtermist solutions naturally include attention to global equity. The framing that longtermism abandons present-justice concerns misunderstands what serious longtermist analysis actually involves.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists argue that longtermism neglects present injustice, they imagine longtermism as caring about abstract future populations while ignoring how harms fall on present ones. But serious longtermist analysis can't ignore distribution. Pandemic risks aren't equally distributed; AI risks aren't equally distributed; climate risks aren't equally distributed. Anyone working seriously on these issues has to engage with present-justice questions about who gets harmed and by whom. The neartermist charge attacks a stripped-down version of longtermism that doesn't engage with the actual analysis.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Civilization-scale risks distribute unequally; serious longtermist analysis must engage with how harms fall.
Pandemic, AI, and climate risks all hit poor and marginalized populations harder; longtermist solutions naturally include equity considerations.
The 'longtermism abandons present justice' framing attacks a stripped-down version that doesn't engage with the actual analysis.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'longtermism includes equity considerations' defense is partly true but doesn't address the resource-allocation pattern. When longtermist analysis recognizes that pandemic risks fall harder on poor populations, the policy implication isn't usually 'fund pandemic-affected communities directly' but 'fund pandemic preparedness research.' The equity recognition exists but tends to be diverted into longtermist priorities rather than driving present-justice work. Acknowledging that risks distribute unequally is good; the framework still systematically prioritizes speculative future work over present-tense distributional response.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists invoke equity considerations to defend against the present-injustice charge, but the considerations function differently in longtermist work than in present-justice work. Where present-justice work would say 'reparations for documented harms,' longtermist work says 'pandemic preparedness research that may benefit affected populations downstream.' Both responses can claim to address inequality, but they have very different resource allocations and different effects on present injustice. The 'we include equity' defense doesn't address what longtermism actually does with the equity recognition.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Longtermist equity recognition typically gets diverted into longtermist priorities rather than present-justice work.
The same recognition that 'risks distribute unequally' produces different resource allocations in longtermist vs present-justice work.
Acknowledging equity considerations isn't the same as acting on them in ways that meaningfully address present injustice.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Some of the most important present injustices are structural — systems of power, technology development, institutional arrangement that produce harm at scale and over time. Longtermist analysis of civilization-scale risks naturally engages with structural questions: who controls AI development, how nuclear authority is distributed, who benefits from biosecurity infrastructure. These structural questions are simultaneously present-justice questions and long-term-trajectory questions; addressing them serves both. The opposition between longtermism and present-justice work breaks down at the structural level where most of the important problems actually live.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who argue against longtermism for ignoring structural injustice often haven't engaged with longtermist work on AI governance, biosecurity, or nuclear policy. These are structural-injustice topics where longtermism has substantial work. Treating longtermism as if it only cared about abstract future populations while ignoring power, control, and distribution is a strawman. The actual analysis longtermists do on these topics engages directly with structural questions, often more carefully than neartermist alternatives do.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Civilization-scale risks involve structural questions: who controls AI development, how nuclear authority is distributed, who benefits from biosecurity infrastructure.
Longtermist analysis on these topics engages with present-structural-injustice questions directly.
The opposition between longtermism and structural-injustice work breaks down where most important problems actually live.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Longtermist engagement with 'structural injustice' tends to focus on technological and governance questions while leaving alone the broader patterns of structural inequality that produce most ongoing harm: economic inequality, racial injustice, gender oppression, colonial legacies. Calling AI governance work 'structural-injustice work' uses the language of present-justice analysis without engaging with what structural-injustice work actually addresses. The longtermist framework picks specific technological-governance issues and labels them structural; the broader work of present-justice analysis isn't part of the longtermist framework.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke 'structural injustice' to describe their work on AI governance or biosecurity, they're using the language of present-justice analysis selectively. Real structural-injustice analysis addresses economic inequality, racial injustice, gender oppression, colonial legacies — broad patterns of systemic harm with documented histories. Longtermism picks specific technological topics and applies the structural-injustice label, but the actual frameworks of present-justice analysis aren't part of how longtermism works. The label is borrowed; the framework is different.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Real structural-injustice analysis addresses economic inequality, racial injustice, gender oppression, colonial legacies.
Longtermism picks specific technological topics for 'structural' analysis without engaging with broader patterns of systemic harm.
The 'structural injustice' label is borrowed selectively; the actual frameworks of present-justice analysis aren't integrated.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Look at what longtermist organizations actually fund. Open Philanthropy gives substantial money to global health and development, criminal justice reform, animal welfare, scientific research with present-tense applications. Effective Altruism communities fund GiveWell-aligned global poverty work alongside longtermist priorities. The empirical allocation pattern shows portfolios that include both present-tense and long-term work, not the abandonment of present-justice work the critique alleges. Treating longtermism as anti-present-justice ignores what the people involved actually do.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Critics of longtermism for neglecting present injustice often haven't actually looked at the funding patterns. Open Philanthropy's grant database shows substantial allocation to global health, criminal justice, animal welfare. EA-aligned communities fund GiveWell charities at hundreds of millions per year. The 'longtermism abandons present-tense work' charge is empirically wrong as a description of the actual movement. It might be true of some abstract longtermist position, but the people implementing the framework in practice don't behave the way the critique describes.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Longtermist organizations like Open Philanthropy fund substantial present-tense work (global health, criminal justice, animal welfare).
EA-aligned communities continue to fund GiveWell-aligned global poverty work at high levels alongside longtermist priorities.
The empirical allocation pattern shows portfolio approaches, not the abandonment alleged by critics.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The defense of longtermism via 'look at the actual funding' counts in some present-tense work and ignores the trends. Longtermist communities have shifted resources increasingly toward speculative work over time. Major donors who began with global health work now allocate substantial fractions to longtermist causes. The portfolios that include present-tense work do so at decreasing proportions. The empirical pattern isn't 'we fund both equally and always have'; it's 'we used to fund mostly present-tense work, now we fund increasingly long-term work, and the trend continues.' That's the trend that produces present-injustice neglect.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists cite their funding of present-tense work, they show a snapshot rather than the trend. The trend in EA-aligned philanthropy is increasing allocation to speculative longtermist work and decreasing relative allocation to present-tense work. Snapshots of present allocations look balanced; trends show systematic shift toward longtermist priorities. The 'we fund both' defense addresses the snapshot; it doesn't address the direction of change, which is what the present-injustice critique is actually about.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: EA-aligned philanthropy shows trend of increasing allocation to longtermist priorities and decreasing relative allocation to present-tense work.
Snapshot defenses ('we fund both') address current state, not the direction of change.
Present-injustice critique is about systematic shift, which the defense doesn't address.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The 'longtermism is biased against present harm' framing assumes a baseline view in which present and long-term considerations get equal weight. But equal weighting wouldn't be principled either — it would just be the inverse bias, an unprincipled compromise between considerations of vastly different magnitudes. Longtermism's weighting toward long-term considerations follows from taking the underlying impartialist principle seriously. If you want to argue against the weighting, the argument has to be against the principle, not against the bias the principle produces. Calling the weighting 'biased' presupposes a baseline that itself isn't defended.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who call longtermism 'biased against present harm' are smuggling in a baseline of equal-weight-to-present-and-future. But this baseline isn't more principled than longtermism's actual weighting; it's just a compromise that splits the difference between two views without grounding the split. If you accept that future people matter, you have to follow through on the weighting their numbers imply. Calling the result 'biased' is just rejecting the conclusion you don't want.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Calling longtermism 'biased' assumes a baseline of equal weight to present and future, which isn't independently defended.
Equal weighting would be its own bias, not a neutral starting point.
Longtermism's weighting follows from taking impartialist principle seriously; calling it bias just rejects the conclusion.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'baseline-bias' defense has the structure of begging the question. Longtermism's weighting is defended by appeal to the impartialist principle, but the impartialist principle is exactly what's contested. If the principle is wrong (or partially wrong, or not the only relevant principle), then the weighting is biased toward considerations that don't deserve the weight. Calling neartermist resistance 'biased toward the present' presupposes that the impartialist principle is correct and complete, which is the contested point. Both sides have framework commitments; only one side gets to claim its framework is the neutral baseline.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists defend their weighting by appeal to impartialist principles, they're treating their framework as neutral. But the impartialist principle that motivates the weighting is one philosophical commitment among several. Other ethical traditions weight present and identifiable concerns more heavily, for principled reasons. The neartermist position isn't 'biased toward present'; it's 'committed to a different framework with its own principled grounds.' Calling neartermist resistance 'bias' assumes the longtermist framework is the neutral one, which is contested.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: The impartialist principle that grounds longtermist weighting is one philosophical commitment among several.
Other ethical traditions weight present and identifiable concerns more heavily on principled grounds.
Calling neartermist resistance 'bias' assumes the longtermist framework is neutral, which is the contested point.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Resistance to longtermism often draws on the identifiable-victim effect — the psychological tendency to feel stronger obligations to people we can specifically picture. This effect is well-documented and well-understood, and it's a known bias in moral cognition. Longtermism asks us to override the identifiable-victim effect when it points the wrong way: when we feel strong obligation to identifiable present sufferers and weak obligation to vast aggregate future ones, we should recognize that the psychological pull doesn't track moral importance. The morally serious response to known biases is to correct for them, not indulge them.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists invoke 'present-justice intuitions' against longtermism, they're often drawing on identifiable-victim psychology rather than principled philosophy. The intuitions feel strong because they're keyed to specific people we can picture, and they feel weak about aggregate future welfare because we can't picture trillions of future people. But moral importance doesn't track psychological vividness, and treating intuitions as if they did is committing a known cognitive error. The neartermist position is partly a defense of unreliable moral cognition.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: The identifiable-victim effect is a well-documented bias that produces stronger obligations to people we can specifically picture.
Longtermism asks us to override this bias when it points the wrong way (toward weaker obligation to vast aggregate populations).
Treating identifiable-victim intuitions as if they tracked moral importance is committing a known cognitive error.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Calling present-justice intuitions 'identifiable-victim bias' rhetorically dismisses one side of a substantive philosophical disagreement. Yes, identifiable-victim psychology exists. But the philosophical commitment that morality is grounded in actual relations to actual people isn't reducible to that psychology. Care ethics, virtue ethics, contractualism all give principled accounts of why obligations to identifiable people are different in kind from obligations to abstract aggregates. Treating these traditions as 'cognitive bias' confuses ethical commitment with psychological irrationality.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists invoke the identifiable-victim effect to dismiss neartermist intuitions, but the move conflates psychology with philosophy. The identifiable-victim effect is a real psychological tendency, yes — but the philosophical commitment that obligations attach to actual relations isn't reducible to the psychology. Care ethics, contractualism, virtue ethics give principled grounds for the commitment that have nothing to do with the bias. Calling the philosophical commitment 'bias' is rhetorical dismissal, not engagement.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Care ethics, contractualism, and virtue ethics give principled grounds for present-relational commitments that aren't reducible to identifiable-victim psychology.
The identifiable-victim effect is real; the philosophical commitment to actual relations isn't merely an expression of it.
Calling philosophical commitments 'cognitive bias' is rhetorical dismissal of substantive philosophical traditions.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The disagreement here is partly about the appropriate scope of moral concern. Longtermism advocates a wide scope: all morally significant beings, present or future, in any community. Neartermism implicitly advocates a narrower scope: present beings, particularly identifiable ones, with diminished weight on distant or speculative ones. Each scope has implications, and the question is which is more defensible. The longtermist scope follows from impartialist commitments most people endorse abstractly; the neartermist scope follows from psychological and relational facts about how moral concern actually develops. The first has cleaner philosophical grounding; the second has cleaner psychological grounding.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who reject longtermism's wide scope of concern often imagine they're defending common-sense ethics, but the scope they're defending isn't actually common-sense — it's a reflection of psychological default that doesn't survive philosophical scrutiny. When asked directly whether future people matter morally, almost everyone says yes. When asked to act on this, most people don't. The psychological scope is narrower than the principled scope, and the disagreement is whether ethics should follow the psychological default or the principled position. Longtermism follows the principle.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Longtermism advocates a wide scope of moral concern grounded in impartialist commitments most people endorse abstractly.
Neartermist scope reflects psychological defaults rather than principled philosophy.
The disagreement is whether ethics follows psychological default or principled position; longtermism follows the principle.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'wide scope' that longtermism advocates isn't more principled than alternative scopes; it's just one philosophical commitment. Care ethics has principled reasons for concentrating obligation on close relations. Communitarian ethics has principled reasons for prioritizing present community. Particularist ethics has principled reasons for resisting universal scope. Calling these positions 'psychological default' rather than 'philosophical commitment' is dismissive of well-developed traditions. The actual disagreement is among different principled positions, not between principle and psychology.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists frame the scope disagreement as 'wide scope (principled) vs narrow scope (psychological default).' But narrow scopes have principled defenses: care ethics, communitarianism, particularism. These traditions ground the narrow scope in considerations beyond psychology — relations of care, community membership, particular relationship. Treating narrow-scope ethics as if it were just psychology dismissed by reflection misrepresents the philosophical landscape.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Care ethics, communitarianism, and particularism give principled grounds for narrow-scope ethics beyond psychology.
These traditions ground narrow scope in relations of care, community, and particular relationship.
Framing the disagreement as wide-principled vs narrow-psychological misrepresents the philosophical landscape.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: When neartermists argue that longtermism abandons present injustice, they often miss the opportunity-cost dimension. Resources spent on present-justice work are resources not spent on long-term work, and vice versa. The relevant question isn't 'does longtermism address present injustice?' but 'what's the appropriate balance, given the relative magnitudes and tractabilities?' On honest examination of magnitudes, long-term considerations dominate; on honest examination of tractabilities, both have roles. The right answer is portfolio allocation, not absolute commitment to either. Longtermism advocates portfolio allocation that takes magnitude seriously; the resistance to it is usually about discomfort with where the magnitudes lead.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: The 'longtermism abandons present injustice' framing assumes that work on present injustice is free — that we could do all the present-justice work we currently do plus all the longtermist work we don't, with no opportunity cost. But resources are finite, and reallocations have real opportunity costs. The actual question is what allocation produces the most good per resource spent. Longtermism's answer isn't 'abandon present injustice' but 'allocate marginal resources to where they have higher expected impact, which is long-term work.' This is a portfolio argument, not an abandonment argument.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Resources are finite; allocation between present-justice and long-term work has real opportunity costs.
The relevant question is appropriate balance given magnitudes and tractabilities, not absolute commitment to either.
Longtermism's portfolio recommendation isn't abandonment of present-justice work; it's marginal-resource allocation to higher-expected-impact work.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: The 'opportunity cost' framing assumes that present and long-term work are commensurable — that we can compare expected impact across them and reallocate accordingly. But the comparison requires assigning expected values to long-term work, which depends on the speculative inputs longtermism uses. If those inputs are weakly grounded, the opportunity-cost calculation is too. The argument 'we should reallocate from present justice to long-term work' depends on having reliable expected-value estimates for the long-term work, which longtermism doesn't actually have.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermist invocations of opportunity cost depend on having calibrated estimates of long-term expected value. Without these, the comparison between present-justice work and long-term work can't be done meaningfully. The 'reallocate to higher-expected-impact work' framing assumes the expected impact is reliably knowable; for longtermist work it isn't. So the opportunity-cost argument runs into the same input-grounding problem as the rest of the framework.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Opportunity-cost comparisons require commensurable expected-value estimates across present and long-term work.
Longtermist long-term expected-value estimates aren't well-calibrated, which undermines the opportunity-cost calculation.
The 'reallocate to higher-expected-impact work' framing assumes inputs that the framework doesn't supply.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Some long-term concerns are also present-justice concerns. Climate change harms present poor populations now, not just future ones. Pandemic preparedness affects present marginalized communities, not just hypothetical future ones. AI development distributes harms unequally now, not just downstream. The framing that pits longtermism against present justice often imagines long-term concerns as exclusively future-oriented, when actually they have substantial present-tense distributional dimensions. Working on these issues seriously serves both longtermist and present-justice goals simultaneously, which means the framing of opposition is partly artificial.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who frame longtermism as opposed to present justice often imagine longtermist work as concerning only future people. But many longtermist priorities have substantial present-tense distributional dimensions: climate already harms vulnerable populations, pandemic risk falls on present poor communities, AI deployment harms present workers and marginalized groups. Working on these is simultaneously long-term-trajectory work and present-justice work. The opposition is partly artificial; the actual work overlaps substantially.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Many longtermist priorities have substantial present-tense distributional dimensions (climate, pandemics, AI).
Working on these is simultaneously long-term-trajectory and present-justice work.
The opposition between longtermism and present-justice is partly artificial; the actual work overlaps.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Yes, some long-term concerns have present-tense distributional dimensions — but this doesn't dissolve the opposition between longtermism and present-justice. Climate work could focus on present-affected communities or on long-term trajectory; the framework choice affects what gets funded and how. Pandemic preparedness could focus on present global health infrastructure or on speculative civilizational risks; the framework choice matters. Saying 'these issues have both dimensions' is true but doesn't address that longtermism systematically favors the long-term framing within these issues. The same topic, treated longtermistically vs presentistically, gets very different policy recommendations.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke the present-tense dimensions of issues like climate and pandemic risk, they're showing that the issues have multiple dimensions — but they're not addressing how longtermism treats those dimensions differently. Climate work in the longtermist framing focuses on civilizational trajectory; in the present-justice framing it focuses on currently-affected communities. These produce different policy recommendations and different resource allocations. The 'both dimensions' framing obscures that longtermism systematically favors one within each issue.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Issues with both dimensions get treated differently in longtermist vs present-justice framings; the framing affects policy and allocation.
Longtermism systematically favors trajectory framing within issues that have present-justice dimensions.
The 'both dimensions' defense obscures the framing-driven differences in actual recommendations.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: The history of effective altruism's evolution shows that present-justice and longtermist work can coexist intellectually and institutionally. The movement started with global poverty work (GiveWell era), expanded to include longtermist concerns (Bostrom, MacAskill era), and now operates across both. The same intellectual community that developed evidence-based global poverty methodology developed careful longtermist analysis. Neither displaced the other entirely; both continue. This is what mature engagement with both kinds of work looks like in practice. Critics who imagine longtermism as opposed to present-justice work are arguing against an earlier strawman of the movement, not the actual current state.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Critics of longtermism for neglecting present-justice often have a fossilized view of EA-aligned communities — imagining them as if they had abandoned global poverty work for AI safety speculation. But these communities continue to fund global poverty work substantially, alongside longtermist work, with the same evidence-based methodology applied to both where it works. The opposition the critique imagines isn't reflected in the actual practice. Engagement with the actual practice would show that the strawman doesn't track reality.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: EA-aligned communities continue substantial global poverty work (GiveWell, evidence-based giving) alongside longtermist work.
The same methodology produced both kinds of work; neither displaced the other.
Critics often argue against an earlier strawman of the movement, not the current state.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: EA-aligned communities continue some present-justice work, but the trajectory and the cultural prestige have shifted. Longtermist work increasingly receives the resources, attention, and intellectual centrality that global-poverty work used to. The community remains diverse, but the center of gravity has moved. Citing continued global-poverty funding as if it answered the present-justice critique misses what the critique is actually about: not that longtermism eliminates present-justice work entirely, but that it systematically diminishes its centrality and resource priority.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists cite continued global-poverty funding to defend against the present-justice critique, they're showing that the work continues — but the critique isn't that the work disappears entirely. The critique is that the work loses centrality, resources, and prestige relative to longtermist priorities. The historical trajectory of EA-aligned communities supports this: global-poverty work was the movement's center; it's increasingly peripheral to longtermist concerns in the same communities. The continued-funding defense addresses a stronger version of the critique than the actual one.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: EA-aligned communities continue global-poverty work but it has shifted from center to periphery relative to longtermist priorities.
The trajectory of resources, attention, and prestige favors longtermist work increasingly.
The continued-funding defense addresses a stronger version of the critique than the actual one (loss of centrality, not disappearance).

political_legitimacy.theme: Whether longtermist policy proposals threaten democratic accountability and legitimate political authority.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Longtermist policy proposals don't threaten democratic legitimacy any more than other long-horizon governance does. Constitutional courts, central banks, environmental regulators, and international treaties all involve democratic delegation to expert bodies with long-horizon mandates. These mechanisms have democratic legitimacy because they emerge from democratic processes (constitutional ratification, legislative establishment, treaty signing) — not because they always defer to immediate majority preference. Longtermist proposals operate within this same tradition of democratic delegation, not against it.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who frame longtermist proposals as anti-democratic implicitly treat democracy as 'whatever immediate majorities prefer.' But this isn't a serious account of democracy; it's a populist caricature. Mature democracies routinely build long-horizon commitments into their structure, precisely because immediate majorities aren't well-positioned to reason about long-term effects. The longtermist proposal is consistent with this democratic tradition; calling it anti-democratic mischaracterizes both the proposal and the tradition.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Constitutional courts, central banks, environmental regulators have long-horizon mandates with democratic legitimacy from their establishment processes.
Mature democracies routinely build long-horizon commitments into their structure; longtermism extends this tradition.
The framing of democracy as 'immediate majority preference' is populist caricature, not serious democratic theory.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Longtermist policy proposals tend to concentrate authority with people claiming expertise about long-term outcomes. The structure of these proposals — expert bodies with long-horizon mandates, constitutional commitments to future generations, technocratic governance of long-term-stakes issues — reduces democratic accountability in important ways. Constitutional courts and central banks at least have long democratic histories and well-defined mandates; longtermist proposals are new, philosophical, and ambitious in scope. Granting them comparable democratic legitimacy assumes they'll work like the established institutions, which is a substantial empirical bet.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: The longtermist defense via 'central banks have democratic legitimacy too' overstates how settled the legitimacy of those institutions actually is. Central bank independence has been contested politically for decades; its legitimacy depends on visible effectiveness within a clearly bounded mandate. Longtermist proposals don't have visible effectiveness yet (they're new) and don't have clearly bounded mandates (they aim at civilizational-scale outcomes). Borrowing legitimacy from established institutions while not having their track records or constraints is overclaiming.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Longtermist proposals concentrate authority with experts claiming long-term knowledge; the democratic-accountability concerns are real.
Established long-horizon institutions (central banks, courts) have track records and bounded mandates; longtermist proposals don't.
Borrowing legitimacy from established institutions while not sharing their constraints is overclaiming.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Democratic systems have always involved delegation: voters elect representatives who delegate to administrators who delegate to specialists. Each layer of delegation involves transferring decision-making to actors better-positioned to make specific kinds of decisions. Longtermist policy proposals fit this pattern, delegating long-horizon decisions to bodies with long-horizon mandates and relevant expertise. The transfer of authority from immediate-majority decision-making to specialized long-horizon bodies isn't anti-democratic; it's how complex democracies actually function. Treating longtermist proposals as uniquely anti-democratic ignores the structural similarity to existing legitimate institutions.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: When neartermists object to longtermist proposals on democratic-accountability grounds, they typically don't object to the comparable mechanisms in central banking, environmental regulation, or judicial review. The objection is selective. Either democratic delegation to specialized long-horizon bodies is legitimate (in which case longtermist proposals are too) or it isn't (in which case major existing institutions need to be rebuilt). The selective application of the democratic-accountability concern to longtermist proposals specifically is rhetorical, not principled.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Democratic delegation to specialized bodies is a standard feature of complex democracies.
Longtermist proposals fit this pattern of delegation to bodies with relevant mandates and expertise.
Selective application of democratic-accountability concerns to longtermist proposals is rhetorical, not principled.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Democratic delegation requires reasonably-bounded mandates, defined accountability mechanisms, and the possibility of democratic correction. Established delegations meet these conditions: central banks have inflation targets and political appointment processes, environmental regulators have legislative mandates and judicial review, courts have constitutional grounding. Longtermist proposals tend to have broad civilizational-scale mandates, contested accountability mechanisms, and unclear correction processes. The structural similarity to established delegations is partial; the conditions that legitimate the established ones don't all apply to longtermist proposals.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: Longtermists invoke central banks and environmental regulators as precedents for democratic delegation, but the precedents don't transfer cleanly. Established delegations have bounded mandates, defined accountability, and clear correction mechanisms. Longtermist proposals have broad mandates, contested accountability, and unclear correction. The structural similarity is partial; the conditions that legitimate established delegations are absent in important ways for longtermist ones.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Established delegations have bounded mandates, defined accountability, and clear correction mechanisms.
Longtermist proposals have broad civilizational-scale mandates, contested accountability, and unclear correction.
The conditions that legitimate established delegations are absent in important ways for longtermist ones.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: One concern raised against longtermist proposals is that they claim to represent future generations who can't actually consent to the representation. This concern is real but applies equally to many accepted democratic practices. Constitutional commitments bind future generations; treaty obligations bind them; environmental commitments bind them. Voting now to commit to long-term obligations is what democracies do. The question isn't whether to make decisions on behalf of future generations (democratic systems already do), but how to do so with appropriate humility and institutional design. Longtermist proposals engage with this question; they don't avoid it.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermist objections to representing future generations sometimes imagine the longtermist proposal as unique in this regard. But democratic systems make decisions on behalf of future generations all the time: constitutional design, treaty obligations, infrastructure decisions, environmental commitments. The question is how to do this responsibly, not whether to do it. Longtermist proposals contribute to this question by suggesting institutional designs that take future-generation interests seriously; the alternative isn't 'don't make decisions affecting future generations' but 'make those decisions less reflectively.'
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Democratic systems already make decisions on behalf of future generations through constitutional, treaty, and infrastructure commitments.
The question is how to do this responsibly, not whether to do it.
Longtermist proposals engage with the question by suggesting institutional designs; the alternative is making such decisions less reflectively.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Existing democratic practices that bind future generations are constrained by present-tense democratic processes (constitutional ratification, treaty negotiation, infrastructure debate). Longtermist proposals tend to add layers that further insulate decisions from present-tense democratic processes. The 'we already make decisions for future generations' point is true but doesn't address the question of how much insulation from present democracy is appropriate. Longtermism systematically argues for more insulation; the legitimate concern is whether that's appropriate given the speculativeness of the projected future-generation interests.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists invoke 'we already make decisions for future generations' to defend their proposals, they elide the question of how much insulation from present democratic processes is appropriate. Existing future-binding decisions emerge from present democratic processes (ratification, negotiation, debate). Longtermist proposals push for additional insulation: bodies whose mandates are harder to revise, processes that resist immediate political pressure, expert authority over speculative future scenarios. The disagreement is about the degree of insulation, and the analogy to existing practices doesn't settle it.
pro_neartermism_supporting_points: Existing future-binding decisions emerge from present democratic processes; longtermist proposals push for additional insulation.
The disagreement isn't whether to bind future generations but how much to insulate the binding from present democracy.
The analogy to existing practices doesn't settle the question of appropriate insulation.

paraphrases.pro_longtermism_core: Some critics worry that longtermist proposals aim to circumvent democratic deliberation in service of urgent civilizational concerns. But this misreads the proposals. Most longtermist institutional work is exactly about building deliberative capacity for long-horizon concerns: not bypassing democracy but extending its capacity to engage with timescales it currently struggles with. The work proposes deliberative bodies, expert advisory processes, structured public engagement on long-horizon issues. This is more deliberation, not less. The framing of longtermism as anti-deliberative misunderstands what the work actually is.
paraphrases.pro_longtermism_against_neartermism: Neartermists who portray longtermist proposals as anti-democratic-deliberation often haven't engaged with the actual proposals. Future-generations commissioners involve deliberative processes. AI governance proposals involve structured public engagement. Long-horizon policy advisory bodies are designed to enhance deliberation, not replace it. Treating longtermism as if it were proposing technocratic shortcuts misrepresents the actual institutional work, which is more deliberative, not less.
pro_longtermism_supporting_points: Most longtermist institutional work proposes building deliberative capacity for long-horizon concerns.
Specific proposals (commissioners, advisory bodies, public engagement) are deliberative, not technocratic shortcuts.
The framing of longtermism as anti-deliberative misrepresents the actual proposals.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_core: Longtermist proposals can include deliberative elements while still concentrating authority with people claiming long-term expertise. Future-generations commissioners involve deliberation, but the deliberative process is shaped by who has standing to participate, who has weight in the deliberation, and who decides what counts as well-deliberated. These structural features tend to favor experts over ordinary citizens, even within deliberative frameworks. Calling the proposals 'more deliberative' is technically accurate but doesn't address whose voices are being amplified through the deliberative structures.
paraphrases.pro_neartermism_against_longtermism: When longtermists describe their proposals as 'more deliberative,' they're describing a feature of the proposals without engaging with whose voices the deliberation amplifies.
